title: Week 5 — Text as Data
text:
Week 5 — Text as Data


Turning a series of short texts into tabular data — lexicons, ML, and LLMs via API — and the ground-truth problem
The second research-focused week. You turn unstructured text into numbers you can analyse, compare how you score text against how AI scores it, and build a small pipeline that scales from 5 texts to hundreds via an API. Running case: post-match football manager interviews.

title: Week 5 — Text as Data
section: Before you come to class (30–60 min)
text:
Before you come to class (30–60 min)


✅ Pre-class checklist



API key — set up an LLM API key (OpenAI or Anthropic). See How to get AI API keys. Budget ~$5. Store the key outside the repo (env var, never commit).
Read — NLP Basics — Text as Data and Introduction to APIs (15 min).
Review terms — token, lexicon, classification, sentiment, ground truth (glossary).
Grab the data — 5-interview practice file and the sentiment scale.

title: Week 5 — Text as Data
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of this unit you will be able to:

Explain the classical NLP pipeline (tokenization → BoW → TF-IDF) and where LLMs fit.
Compare the four ways to score sentiment: pre-built lexicons, custom lexicons, ML models, LLMs.
Score text by hand and by AI, and reason about agreement and ground truth.
Build a small text→data pipeline that calls an LLM API at scale, with a reusable prompt.

title: Week 5 — Text as Data
section: Task block (100 min · individual or pairs)
text:
Task block (100 min · individual or pairs)
Scale up from 5 texts to a real pipeline. Start small, validate, then expand.


🎯 Build a text → data pipeline



Get the corpus. Use the combined interview dataset (text_id level) from the interviews case study. One row per text.
Design the prompt. Decide the scale/labels, how to handle irrelevant text, and an output schema (e.g. score, reason, confidence). Prefer structured output over free text. Sketch in sentiment guidelines.
Validate before scaling. Hand-label ~20 texts, run the prompt, compare. Aim for ≥ 80% agreement; if below, revise the prompt before going further.
Classify via API. Call an LLM API over the full set. Reference: Calling LLM APIs from Python, and the case-study Python / R implementations.
Compare methods. Put human average, domain-lexicon score, and AI average side by side. Where do they disagree most?
Stretch. Ask the AI to predict the match result (win/draw/loss) or speaker gender from text alone — and discuss what linguistic cues it’s using and whether they’re reliable.









Tip



APIs beyond LLMs. Getting the data often means data APIs too. If you want practice: World Bank + FRED walkthrough and the FBref football walkthrough. How APIs work under the hood: api-advanced.

title: Guidelines for Rating:
text:
Positive mentions include praise, satisfaction with performance, optimistic outlook, and appreciation.
Negative mentions include frustration, disappointment, criticism of performance, or external conditions.
Neutral statements are neither positive nor negative.


Examples:

“I’m extremely proud of how the team played today. Fantastic performance by everyone.” → +2
“We played well, but there are still areas to improve.” → +1
“It was a tough match, evenly balanced, nothing much to say.” → 0
“We weren’t at our best; it was a frustrating game.” → -1
“I’m very disappointed. Our performance was unacceptable.” → -2



Final Notes:

Use 0 if unsure or if sentiment is mixed without clear dominance.

title: Week 3 — Data Wrangling & Debugging
text:
Week 3 — Data Wrangling & Debugging


Agentic CLI workflows on a real repo — project instructions, skills, tests, git, and the discipline of reviewing what the AI did
The longest hands-on session in the course. AI writes code fast, but output that looks right isn’t always right. This unit does two things at once: it makes you fluent with an agentic CLI tool working across a multi-file project, and it drills the habits that turn a clever assistant into a reproducible research companion — project instruction files, reusable skills, tests, git, and documentation — all wrapped in the discipline of reviewing what the AI did.
The whole session runs on one continuous case study — the Austrian Hotels dataset — so each step builds on the last.

title: Week 3 — Data Wrangling & Debugging
text:
Intro (50 min)


⚡ Why a CLI agent if Copilot already works?


In Units 1–2 you used VS Code + Copilot and Claude Code. The jump here is not “AI vs no AI.” It is IDE assistance vs terminal-native execution. With Copilot the loop is still manual:

Ask for code in the editor → 2. run it in the terminal → 3. read the logs/errors yourself → 4. go back and re-prompt. Repeat.

A CLI agent compresses that loop:

Files are already there. Claude Code sees your CSVs, scripts, and outputs directly — no uploading, no copy-paste. Just: “Look at these files and calculate average occupancy by city.”
Code runs immediately. It writes code, executes it, sees the error, and fixes it — you get results, not just snippets.
Context stays intact. It remembers your project structure and how files relate (hotels.csv joins to cities.csv) across many steps.
Iteration is fast. “Something looks wrong” → it investigates without you shuttling data around.

What stays exactly the same: prompting discipline, statistical thinking (you still define variables, assumptions, checks), verification habits (joins, units, missing values), and the iteration mindset. What changes is only the execution surface — you remain responsible for quality.




🔍 Trust but verify — the operating discipline


Reviewing AI-written code. Common failure modes to hunt for:

Wrong join type — “How many rows before and after the join? Did we lose data?”
Missing values — “Are there NaNs? Where did they come from?”
Plausible-but-wrong — a result that looks right but isn’t. Ask: “Walk me through the calculation step by step.”
Hallucinated code or stats. Always verify against the data.

Good habit, every time: Explain the code you just wrote. What assumptions did you make?
Always check: row counts after joins; summary statistics (do the means make sense?); a few random rows (do the values look realistic?).




📋 Project instruction files (CLAUDE.md / agents.md)


Instead of repeating preferences in every prompt, write them once in a file the harness reads automatically: CLAUDE.md (Claude Code), GEMINI.md (Gemini CLI), AGENTS.md/agents.md (Codex and others).
## Code Style
- Use tidyverse for R; pandas for Python
- Prefer ggplot2 / matplotlib with the viridis palette

## Data Standards
- Dates in ISO 8601 (YYYY-MM-DD); column names lowercase_with_underscores

## Analysis Preferences
- Always check for missing values before analysis
- Report sample sizes in every table
Hierarchical loading: global defaults → project file → subfolder file. More specific files override general ones.




🛠️ Skills, tests, git & autonomy



Skills — reusable instruction sets the agent runs on demand. A project skill lives at .claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md; a personal one at ~/.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md. Then typing /<name> runs the workflow consistently.
Tests = guardrails. Turn assumptions into assertions across raw → clean → analysis: schema/type, completeness (not-null), validity (0 ≤ occupancy ≤ 100), relationships (foreign keys exist), volume (row-count range). Prefer tests that return the failing rows, not just pass/fail.
Git — version control + AI = traceable, reproducible analysis. Branch, change, commit with a clear message, inspect the diff. The agent can also read git history to explain why a past decision was made.
Autonomous execution — fine for trusted, repetitive pipelines with a clear success criterion; risky for new code or shared resources. Always: confirm the branch, write a success criterion, inspect git diff after, and run tests.

title: Week 3 — Data Wrangling & Debugging
section: Task block (100 min · individual or pairs)
text:
Task block (100 min · individual or pairs)
Running case: the Austrian Hotels dataset — messy data plus AI-generated code that has bugs. Work in a git project folder; commit as you go. Verify after every step.


🗂️ 1. Set up & explore as linked tables


Launch the agent in your project folder:
cd austrian-hotels-data
claude

“What files are in this folder? Give me a quick overview.”
“Show me 5 sample rows from each CSV file.”
“Read the hotels and cities files. How are they related? What’s the join key?”

Check: you can name each table, its grain, and the keys (city links hotels→cities; hotel_id links hotels→monthly occupancy).




🧹 2. Find the bugs & clean



Discuss first: what are the crucial steps when cleaning tabular data?
Use the agent to inspect the provided code: check row counts around joins, hunt missing values, standardise team/city names, dates, and keys.
Produce clean tables in a new /data_cleaned folder.





🔗 3. Join, aggregate & investigate


Quick refresher: Joining Tables Guide.

Join — “Join the hotels and cities data. How many hotels are in each province?”
Aggregate — “What’s the average occupancy rate by city? Show a table sorted highest to lowest.”
Investigate — “Which 5-star hotels have the lowest average daily rate? Something seems off — investigate.”

Tips: if something looks wrong, ask “Why did that happen?” or “Check the row counts.” Ask to see intermediate steps: “Show me the data after the join, before aggregating.” Then open a created table manually and look into it — how would you test and debug it yourself?




✨ 4. The power move — generate new data


One of the most useful CLI capabilities is generating realistic synthetic data. (The Austrian Hotels dataset itself was generated by an earlier Claude!)
I want to create a new CSV file called hotel_bookings.csv that shows what
percentage of each hotel's bookings come from different channels (Direct,
Booking.com, Expedia, HRS, Travel Agent). Percentages must sum to 100% per
hotel; 5-star hotels skew to Direct (35–45%), 3-star to OTAs (Booking.com 40%+);
add a commission rate (Direct = 0%, OTAs = 10–18%). Write Python code that uses
hotels_modified.csv as input, run it, and show me a summary.
Then verify: do percentages sum to 100? Are the patterns realistic? Can you join it back to hotels? Be more specific to get realistic patterns. Brainstorm one more join table of your own (weather by city/month, staff by hotel, nearby attractions by city…) and generate it.




📋 5. Set conventions — write CLAUDE.md / agents.md


Create a project instruction file (style, data standards, analysis preferences — see the intro example). Re-run one analysis prompt and notice how the behaviour changes now that conventions are automatic.




🤖 6. Build a skill


Create .claude/skills/clean-hotels-data/SKILL.md:
---
name: clean-hotels-data
description: Clean and validate Austrian Hotels data for analysis.
---

Run the Austrian Hotels cleaning pipeline:
1. Check missing values in `data/hotels_raw.csv`
2. Run the cleaning script
3. Verify output dimensions in `data/hotels_clean.csv`
4. Generate a short data-quality report
Now typing /clean-hotels-data runs the workflow consistently. What other repetitive tasks could become skills?




✅ 7. Write tests (guardrails)


Ask the CLI to generate and run ~5 tests for the cleaning pipeline:

hotel_id is unique in the cleaned table
key fields not null (hotel_id, city_id, date)
city_id values exist in the city lookup table (foreign key)
occupancy_rate between 0 and 100
row count within an expected range after cleaning/joining

Review one failing test together, fix the underlying cause, and rerun. Prefer tests that return the failing rows so you can inspect those exact rows first.




🌿 8. Git + a peek at autonomy



“Create a branch hotels-robustness-checks, run the robustness checks, and prepare a summary of changes.” Then inspect the diff and explain every changed file to a partner.
“Look at the git history for the cleaning script. Why did we change the outlier threshold?” — the agent reads commit messages and diffs.
Autonomy, carefully. A non-interactive run looks like:

claude -p "Run the /clean-hotels-data skill and the robustness checks, then summarize changed files"
Apply the safety protocol: right branch, written success criterion, git diff after, tests after. Only on familiar, verified pipelines — never on new code or shared resources.




📄 9. Document


Write a README / DATA.md: each table, its source, schema, and known issues. This is what lets someone else (or future you) rerun the whole thing.

title: Week 3 — Data Wrangling & Debugging
text:
Operation tips

Use git-based projects. CLI tools are file-based, so git gives safer iteration and easy rollbacks.
A reliable three-step loop: Inventory (“What files are here?”) → Plan (“What steps should we run?”) → Execute and verify.
Read error messages before re-prompting — often the agent fixes errors itself if you just let it run.

Bottom line — CLI shines for: complex multi-file pipelines (raw → clean → analysis → exhibits), reproducible workflows others can run, large datasets/documents needing context, and iterative analysis where the AI tests and debugs autonomously. IDE/chat is still better for: quick one-off questions, exploratory methodology conversations, and moments when you want tight control over each step.

title: Week 1 — LLMs, Harnesses & Setup
text:
Week 1 — LLMs, Harnesses & Setup


What is actually behind the chat box, when a paid subscription is worth it, what a harness adds — and getting one running on your machine
This week starts where most people actually are: you have used the free ChatGPT (or Claude, or Gemini) in a browser, and that’s it. That is a fine starting point — but it is roughly like having only ever used a calculator when a spreadsheet exists. By the end of this session you will understand what an LLM actually does, what happens when you share a document with one, when paying $20/month is worth it (and when it isn’t), what a harness is and why it changes everything for data work — and you will have at least one harness installed and working on your own machine.
This is the one lecture-heavy week. Everything after this is hands-on.

title: Week 1 — LLMs, Harnesses & Setup
section: Chunk 1 — What’s behind the chat box (40 min · talk)
text:
Chunk 1 — What’s behind the chat box (40 min · talk)


📊 Core LLM concepts — no math required


Slideshow: LLM Concepts and Applications

What an LLM is — a statistical model that predicts the next token (word piece) given everything so far, trained on a huge slice of human text. No database of facts, no lookup — prediction. This one idea explains both the magic and the failure modes.
Tokens — models don’t see words or characters; they see tokens (~¾ of a word in English). Everything is metered in tokens: what you can fit in, what you pay for via API, how fast it responds.
The transformer — how 2017’s “Attention Is All You Need” made today’s models possible. You don’t need the details; you need the consequence: the model attends to everything in its context at once.
Training & feedback — pre-training on text, then instruction-tuning and human feedback (RLHF). This is why models are helpful and polite, and also why they’d rather produce a confident wrong answer than say “I don’t know.”
The jagged frontier — LLMs are superhuman at some tasks and surprisingly bad at adjacent ones, and the boundary is invisible until you test it. See Mollick on AI jaggedness.
Cyborg vs Centaur — two ways to split work with AI (Mollick): the Centaur hands off whole sub-tasks; the Cyborg interleaves human and AI move-by-move. You’ll feel both this term.

The model landscape (details in Which AI model):

Frontier closed models — Claude (Anthropic), GPT (OpenAI), Gemini (Google). State of the art; you rent them per month or per token.
Open-weights models — Llama, Qwen, Mistral, DeepSeek, Kimi. You can download the weights and run them yourself; think of them as roughly SOTA-minus-a-few-months. Why they matter: privacy, cost at scale, reproducibility. We return to them at the end of today.





🧠 The context window — the concept that explains almost everything


The context window is the model’s working memory: everything it can “see” at once — your messages, its answers, any files you shared. Current frontier models handle roughly 200K–1M tokens (a few hundred pages), and models are typically stronger early in the window than when it is stuffed full.
What follows from this single concept:

A new chat is a blank slate. The model does not remember yesterday’s conversation (unless the app injects a “memory” summary — that’s a product feature, not the model).
Long chats degrade. As the window fills up, earlier details get crowded out or attended to poorly. For serious work: start fresh chats per task, and re-state what matters.
What happens when you upload a document: the file is converted to tokens and placed into the context window. Nothing is “learned”; the model reads it like a very fast skimmer. A 30-page PDF fits comfortably. A 180 MB CSV does not — the app will silently truncate, sample, or use a code tool to peek at it. If you don’t know which happened, you can’t trust the answer.
This is why data workflows need more than chat. Real datasets don’t fit in a context window. The professional pattern — which this whole course teaches — is: give the model the codebook, column lists, and small samples, and have it write code that processes the full data outside the window.

Privacy — where your documents go. An uploaded file goes to the provider’s servers. On consumer plans, chats may be used to train future models depending on your data settings — check them (ChatGPT: Settings → Data controls; Claude: privacy settings). Paid business/enterprise tiers and API access come with stronger no-training guarantees. House rule for this course: nothing confidential goes into a chat you wouldn’t put in an email to an outside company.

title: Week 1 — LLMs, Harnesses & Setup

text:
Chunk 2 — Free vs paid, and what a harness adds (40 min · talk + demo)


💳 Free vs paid — the honest comparison


All major providers run the same ladder. Prices as of mid-2026 (check current pages before subscribing):









Tier
ChatGPT
Claude
What you actually get




Free
$0 (with ads in some countries)
$0
Limited messages that fall back to smaller models when you hit the cap; limited file upload; smallest context; fine for casual questions


Budget
Go — ~$8/mo
—
More messages on mid-tier models


Standard
Plus — $20/mo
Pro — $20/mo
The full frontier models incl. extended thinking, deep research, projects, big file uploads, and the coding agent (Codex / Claude Code)


Power
Pro — $100–200/mo
Max — $100–200/mo
5×–20× the usage limits, best-model access all day



(Gemini has the same shape: free tier and Google AI Pro at ~$20/mo. GitHub Copilot is the outlier: ~$10/mo, free for verified students and teachers.)
What the free tier really costs you for data work: you get routed to smaller models mid-conversation, you can’t attach much, deep research and thinking modes are capped or absent — and crucially, you don’t get the coding agent.
When should you subscribe? A rule of thumb:

If you use AI a few times a week to look things up or draft a paragraph → free is fine.
If you do analytical work (coding, data, writing reports) more than ~2–3 hours a week → the $20 tier pays for itself in the first afternoon. One consultant-hour costs more.
The $100+ tiers are for people who run agents much of the day. You will not need them for this course.
For this course, a $20 tier that includes a coding agent is effectively required — that’s Claude Pro or ChatGPT Plus (or student Copilot).





🔧 Harnesses — the model is the engine, the harness is the car


A harness is the software wrapped around a model that lets it actually do things. The chat website is one harness — the simplest one. A coding agent like Claude Code, Codex, or Copilot is a different harness around the same model, and it is the reason this course exists.
Here is what changes, on the same $20 subscription:









Chat app (browser)
Harness / coding agent




Files
You upload them one by one, into the context window
It reads your folders directly — a whole project of CSVs, scripts, PDFs, hundreds of files, fetching what it needs when it needs it


Code
Writes snippets; maybe runs them in a remote sandbox
Writes, runs, and debugs code on your machine, sees the error, fixes it, reruns


Output
Text you copy-paste
Real files: edited scripts, saved figures, cleaned CSVs, reports


Tools
Fixed set (search, maybe a sandbox)
Tool use: shell, git, package installs, web fetch, your own scripts, MCP connectors


Scale of work
One answer per prompt
Agentic loops: plans multi-step tasks, works for minutes to hours, can manage sub-agents working in parallel


Memory across sessions
Product “memory,” opaque
Instruction files you control (CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md): project conventions the agent reads every time



So: the $20 chat subscription answers questions; the same $20 pointed at a harness does the work with you — on a great deal of material, in your folders, with tools, verifiably. The trade: it runs on your machine with real permissions, so you also learn safety habits (it asks before running commands; you review diffs; git is your undo button).
The three harnesses on the menu today (skills transfer 1:1 between them):

Awareness, not required: there are also open-code harnesses — open-source agents you point at any model, including a local one. Same workflow, swappable engine.

text:
Closing talk — beyond subscriptions: OpenRouter & local models


🌐 OpenRouter — one key, every model


Subscriptions are one door to the models; the other is the API — pay per token, no monthly fee. OpenRouter is a marketplace that puts hundreds of models (frontier and open-weights) behind one API key and one bill. Why an analyst cares:

Compare models on your task — run the same prompt through Claude, GPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, Kimi and diff the answers.
Cheap bulk work — classifying 100,000 texts (as in our capstone) through an open-weights model can cost a few dollars instead of a few hundred.
One integration — most harnesses and libraries accept an OpenRouter endpoint; you swap models by changing one string.

We use APIs seriously in Week 5 and the capstone — see Get AI API keys when you get there.




🦙 Running an open-weights model on your own computer


The final rung of independence: download the weights, run the model locally. Nothing leaves your machine — the answer to privacy, offline work, and perfectly reproducible (“frozen”) models. The easy on-ramp is Ollama or LM Studio.
What machine do you need? The model must fit in your GPU memory (VRAM) or a Mac’s unified memory:








Model size
Hardware needed
What it’s like




3–4B
Any modern laptop, 8 GB RAM
Autocomplete-plus; fine for drafts and simple extraction


7–8B
16 GB RAM laptop or 8 GB VRAM GPU
Genuinely useful for summarising, classification, simple code


14–32B
24 GB VRAM GPU (RTX 4090/5090-class) or 32 GB+ Apple Silicon
Solid mid-tier assistant; the sweet spot for local


70B
48–64 GB — big GPU rig or 64–128 GB Mac
Approaches last year’s frontier


Frontier-scale open models (DeepSeek, Kimi)
Server-class, multiple GPUs
Don’t run these at home — rent them via OpenRouter



Try it if curious: ollama run llama3.2 and give it the Connecticut prompt. Feel the capability gap versus the frontier model — that gap is the price of privacy. Full orientation: Open-weights & local models.

2. The causal question


🎯 What are we actually trying to answer?


Research question: Does changing a manager improve team performance? And does the impact vary by manager and team characteristics?
Your first task is to translate it into a very specific question you will estimate.

Define all aspects of the question
Make editorial decisions.

sample design

title: Capstone Project — Session 3: Causal Analysis & Final Presentation
text:
3. Building the analysis panel


🧩 Your two datasets don’t quite fit together


You arrive at Session 3 with two outputs:
From Session 1:

a match/manager-change panel. Rows indexed by some combination of team, season, date, match_id.
team characteristics
manager characteristics

From Session 2:

an article-level table
a (team, gameweek) → avg_score aggregation.

Potential issues
We have to create a single panel dataset.
A short list of what to expect:

Entity resolution
Time unit problems, inconsistencies and mismatch
Coverage gaps regarding the expectation data
Date alignment

These are not bugs in your pipeline. They are the substance of working with real data. Fixing them is the first half of this session. Don’t start the regression until you have a merge you trust.




🏗️ Decisions you have to name (write them in PANEL.md)


Before you merge anything, pick and write down your answers to these:

Unit of observation. (team, match)? (team, calendar_week)? (team, gameweek)?
Time index.
Entity keys. One clean team identifier across all tables. One clean manager identifier.
Treatment timing. What is “the” date of the change.
Pre / post window. How many periods before and after the change do you include? 5 matches? 10 weeks? To end of season?
Missing-coverage policy. A (team, week) with zero articles: do you drop it, impute zero, or carry forward the previous week’s score?

None of these has a universally right answer. But you do need to commit to one answer per question and defend it in the slides.

title: Capstone Project — Session 3: Causal Analysis & Final Presentation
text:
4. Difference-in-Differences — vocabulary & tools
This is a vocabulary to get started. You can learn the rest with AI — not a from-scratch DiD lecture.


📐 Key concepts


Setup

Treatment — the event whose effect you want to measure. Here: a manager change.
Treated unit — a team that experiences a manager change. Control unit — a team that does not (in the same window).

Methods

Two-way fixed effects (team FE + time FE) — the standard panel regression that could be a good start.
Event-study specification — transform data into event time (when the intervention happens); one coefficient per lead / lag around the event, to see the dynamics rather than a single number.
Pre / post — periods before vs after the change.
DiD estimator — the difference between treated and control in the change from pre to post. In plain words: how much more (or less) did treated teams’ performance move than control teams’?

Key challenges

Parallel trends — the core assumption: absent treatment, treated and control would have moved in parallel. Mostly untestable, but pre-trends are a useful proxy.
Staggered treatment — different teams are treated at different times. This has important econometric implications that you shall investigate.
Ask AI on what can go wrong with a naive DiD in your setup.





📦 Package pointers


Python

diff-diff — a general difference-in-differences / event-study package with sensible defaults. New but already great.
pyfixest — general regression package with options for difference in differences.

R (if you prefer)

did — the original Callaway–Sant’Anna implementation.
fixest — fastest FE in the ecosystem; feols, etable, coefplot.









Tip



Use AI to learn the details
— ask for worked mini-examples in your setup. Then read the code, don’t just run it. - Use the AI-interviews-me technique to better understand the setup, what you expect, and what your key modelling choices are.

title: Capstone Project — Session 3: Causal Analysis & Final Presentation
text:
5. The expectations angle


🧭 What is the purpose of knowing if a manager change was expected?


Look at data

Focus on the season(s) you have data on expectations.
Descriptive: What share of changes were expected? Were there cases when expectation was high but the manager was not fired?

Econometrics

Parallel trends: what does it mean in this context?
What does it mean to have anticipation in terms of the causal estimation?

Use

Heterogeneity: do expected changes have a different effect than unexpected ones?

Compare dynamics and simple diff-in-diffs estimates.

title: Capstone Project — Session 3: Causal Analysis & Final Presentation
text:
6. Analysis work block (90 min)


🔬 Suggested workflow


Here is a suggested workflow. But you can proceed differently.

Merge & validate. Join Session 1 and Session 2 on your chosen keys. Print counts before and after. Eyeball a few rows.
Write the spec — in METHODS.md, before any regression:

Outcome.
Unit.
Treatment definition (date, caretaker handling).
Window (pre/post periods).
Controls (team FE, time FE, opponent strength).
Cluster level for SEs (team).

Test on a subset — one season. Get the plumbing right before you scale.
Try out one or two models — think about what econometric models you shall use. Start with something you understand.
Test additional econometric model — think about time, dynamics. Carefully interact with AI to pick one or two extra models.
Heterogeneity 1 — interact with a binary indicator of manager characteristic. Repeat for team characteristic.
Expectations — interact with expectation score.
Robustness — think about 2 key decisions you have made. Test how much they matter.
Draft slides while code runs. Don’t leave them for the last 15 minutes.

title: Part 3: A Paper in 50 Minutes
text:
Part 3 of 6 · live demo


A Paper in 50 Minutes


One prompt, a short empirical paper and a slide deck. While the agent works, we look at the prompt: what it asks for, and what it leaves out

title: Part 3: A Paper in 50 Minutes
text:
What happens in this part?
In Part 2 we went step by step: one task, one check, then the next task. Here we do the opposite. We give the agent a single prompt, and it runs a whole project, from the question and the data to a short paper and a slide deck.
The question is close to the one in Part 2: does the World Cup change the number of births? In Part 2 you read what researchers found about big events and births. The agent was told to ignore that literature and build its own design. So you come to its paper as a referee who has done the reading.
We start the agent and, while it works, we look at the prompt: what it asks for, and what it leaves out. Your own part comes after the session, in the Assignment.






NoteThe project folder



We share the complete project folder, as the agent left it, with the participants after the session: the paper, the slides, the decision memo, the code and the data. You will work with it in the Assignment.

title: Part 3: A Paper in 50 Minutes
text:
What is in the prompt?
Here is the prompt, exactly as we gave it, typos included.
## about

Does the World Cup affect fertility? 

Let us write an economics paper that investigates the causal effect of football world cups on birth rates. 

The paper should target an economics journal. But make it digestible for other social scientists especially in terms of the context and contribution. 

Maybe frame it such that  world cups are an allegory for something more general. 

## tasks

1. Setup: Use current folder to set up folder structure. 
2. Data: Find fertility across countries. Find football world cup data. save raw data. 
3. Methods: Use well designed econometrics and credible identification strategies. Make sure we think about key mechanism(s). 
4. Exhibits: Make beatiful graphs and tables as exhbits -- you'll use them in a presentation and in a paper. 
5. You can use Python or R. Just ensure nice human readable codebase. Install python / R packages when needed. 
6. Output1: Write an academic paper. It should be 10-15 pages + references. It should have 8-15 references. 
7. Output2: Turn paper into slides. Create PDF slide deck.  
8. Decisions_md: create an internal memo that is a list with all key decisions you made, could be about story, mechanisms, identification strategy, model specification, data use and so on. When (if) relevant the file should include debates among your agents, disagreements, and how a decision was reached.
9. There may be papers, dissertations, blogposts on this exact task. Disregard them, don't read them, don't cite them at this initial stage. You can collect them, store them, just don't use or build on them.
Note what it specifies: a question, an audience, nine tasks, the outputs, and a memo of decisions. Note also what it leaves open: which data, which countries, which years, which method. Each of those is a choice the agent has to make on its own.
Some of the tasks do the work of rules. Save raw data keeps the originals. Human readable codebase asks for code you can follow. The decisions memo is the DECISIONS.md of Part 2. And the last task tells the agent to ignore the existing literature, so that the design is its own.

title: Part 3: A Paper in 50 Minutes
section: What is not in the prompt?
text:
What is not in the prompt?
In Part 2 the agent worked with standing rules (AGENTS.md) and with skills. Here we left both out, to see what a bare prompt gives. The agent starts in an empty folder: there is no rules file, and the prompt calls no skill.
Three things are missing, and it is worth noticing them before the agent starts.
A stop. The prompt never says “show me the plan and wait”. The agent chooses the data, the sample and the method, and goes on.
A review. Nobody reads the results with fresh eyes before the paper is written, and nobody reruns the code after it. In Step 2.5 we asked a new session to review a one-page memo. Here a whole paper gets no review.
A check of the references. The prompt asks for 8 to 15 references, and it does not ask the agent to verify any of them.
True, the agent may do some of this on its own. But what a prompt doesn’t ask for, you can’t count on. In the Assignment you will put these pieces back, with skills.

title: Part 3: A Paper in 50 Minutes
section: What does the agent leave behind?
text:
What does the agent leave behind?
A project folder, in the structure it chose: the raw and the cleaned data, the scripts, the charts and tables, the paper, the slide deck, the decisions memo and a README. It is close to the structure of your first-project, a bit larger. Follow how it fills up during the demo.

title: Part 3: A Paper in 50 Minutes
text:
What is a 50-minute paper worth?
What you will see looks like a paper: a question, data, tables, charts, a conclusion. But it is a first draft, made in under an hour, and nobody has checked it yet. Don’t judge it as a finished paper, and don’t take its results at face value.
The point of the demo is the process: how far the agent gets on its own, and how much work is left for you before your name could go on the result.
Note what the agent doesn’t bring, too. The question comes from us. So does the judgment on whether the answer is interesting, and whether it is right.

title: Part 3: A Paper in 50 Minutes
section: What should you watch during the demo?
text:
What should you watch during the demo?
Four things are worth following as the agent works.
The plan. Before it touches anything, the agent proposes a plan. Is it the plan you would have made?
The choices. Each time the agent picks a sample, a definition or a method, ask yourself whether you would have picked the same.
The checks. Does it test its own work, as in Step 2.3? What does it do when a check fails?
The files. Follow what gets written where: data, code, outputs, the decision memo, the paper.

title: Part 3: A Paper in 50 Minutes
text:
What comes next?
The demo ends when the agent stops. Your part starts there, at home, with the Assignment. First you read the project folder as a referee would. Then you improve the prompt with skills, so that the next run gets the stop, the review and the reference check that this one did not have.

Continue with the Assignment →

title: Part 5: Go Further
text:
Part 5 of 6 · broader advice, for self-study


Go Further


Beyond the case study: more kinds of work, a voice of your own, freedom from one provider, and a model that fits the task

title: Part 5: Go Further
text:
What is this part?
Parts 1 to 4 were a guided path around one case study. This part is different. It collects broader advice for the time when the agent is part of your work: what else to use it for, and how to choose your tools. There are no steps to follow and nothing to finish. Read what is relevant to you, and skip the rest.

What else can I use it for?
How do I make it write like me?
Should I depend on one provider?
Which model for which task?
What about confidential material?

We will add more over time.

title: Part 5: Go Further
section: What else can I use it for?
text:
What else can I use it for?
Once the routines of Part 2 feel normal, try the agent on work that is not analysis. Which tasks are worth trying? Two questions help. Is the material in files that the agent can read? And can you check the result in less time than the work would take you? If the answer to both is yes, try it.
Two uses we like, both adapted from Simon Martin’s Jump-starting AI agents:
A sparring partner. Test an argument before you take it to colleagues or start writing it up. The agent often spots what you missed, such as a clash with an earlier section.

I think Section 5 of docs/draft.md should be reframed as follows: [your idea]. Assess this critically against the rest of the draft and the papers in docs/readings/. List the weakest points first.

Admin. Progress reports, applications, forms: tasks where the information exists in your files but has to be pulled together.

Draft the progress report from the documents in docs/funding/. Follow the structure of docs/funding/report-template.docx. Write it in Markdown first, and mark anything you could not find in the documents with TODO.

For more ideas, see the useful links in the overview. The first group there is for people who don’t code.

title: Part 5: Go Further
section: How do I make it write like me?
text:
How do I make it write like me?
Out of the box, the agent writes generic prose: smooth, correct, and not like you, nor like the papers in your field. Readers notice. The fix is the same as everywhere in this course: give it grounding material.
Put one or two of your own papers in docs/samples/, as PDFs or Word files. Then start a new session and send:

Read the papers in docs/samples/. Write a short note in docs/my-voice.md on how I write: sentence length, how I state results and caveats, words I use and words I avoid, with two or three short examples from the samples. Then add a line to AGENTS.md saying that any text you write for me should follow docs/my-voice.md.

Read docs/my-voice.md and correct it: it is a description of you, so you are the judge. For the conventions of your field (notation, how results are stated), point the agent to the papers in docs/readings/ in the same way. When the note has settled, it is a good candidate for a skill (Step 4.3): “Turn docs/my-voice.md into a skill called my-voice.”

title: Part 5: Go Further
section: Should I depend on one provider?
text:
Should I depend on one provider?
In this course the agent was Claude Code. It has two parts, and it helps to tell them apart.

The desktop application is the program on your computer that reads files, runs commands and asks for your permission. In the AI community these applications are called harnesses.
The model is the AI behind it, which does the thinking.

So far both came from one company: the Claude app works with Anthropic’s models only. But the two parts can be separated. OpenCode is an open-source application that works much like Claude Code, and it works with models from many providers. You choose the model from a menu.
Why does this matter? Because providers change. Prices go up, usage limits get tighter, a model you rely on is retired, or your university signs a contract with another company. If your app works with any model, you switch the model and keep everything else: your project folders, your AGENTS.md, your skills and your habits.
You don’t have to switch now. Our advice is more modest: keep what you build in plain files, as this course did, so that it is not tied to one company. And try a second app once, so you know the way.






NoteSetting up OpenCode (click to open)





It takes about ten minutes. What you built in this course carries over: OpenCode reads the AGENTS.md in your project folder, and it finds the skills in .claude/skills/ by itself.

Install the desktop app. The download links for Windows, Mac and Linux are on the first page of the OpenCode documentation. There is also a terminal version, which works the same way.
Open a copy of your project. Make a copy of first-project, call it first-project-opencode, and open that folder. Then the two applications can’t get in each other’s way, and you can compare their results side by side.
Make it ask first. OpenCode is more permissive than Claude Code in Manual mode: it may change files and run commands without asking. To get the behaviour you know, save a file called opencode.jsonc in the project folder, with this content:

{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "permissions": [
    { "action": "edit", "resource": "*", "effect": "ask" },
    { "action": "shell", "resource": "*", "effect": "ask" },
    { "action": "external_directory", "resource": "*", "effect": "ask" }
  ]
}
The three lines say: ask before changing a file, ask before running a command, and ask before touching anything outside the project folder.
OpenCode also has the two ways of working you know. They are called agents here: Build does the work, and Plan proposes without changing your files. In the terminal version, Shift+Tab switches between them.
The app needs a model before it can do anything. See the box in the next section.

title: Part 5: Go Further
text:
Which model for which task?
In Part 1 the choice was among Anthropic’s models. With an app that works with any model, the choice is wider. Many strong models are open-weights: their makers publish the trained model, so any company can run it and sell access to it. Competition keeps the price low.
We find it useful to think of three kinds of model. Each has its use.



Kind
Example
Use it for




Cheap open-weights
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash
Simple tasks repeated many times: sorting texts into categories, pulling a few facts out of each document


Very good
Claude Opus 5.5
Most research work: extracts with quotes, a memo, a data task


State of the art
Claude Fable 5.2
The hardest and longest tasks: a whole project from one prompt, as in Part 3, or the review of a finished paper



There is a fourth option, too. High-end open-weights models, such as Kimi K3.1 Pro, cost about half as much as Claude Opus 5.5 at list prices (November 2026). Where one of them does a task well enough, it saves money.
Which kind fits which task is not fixed. It depends on the task, on your field and on how costly a mistake would be, and it changes with every new model. So we advise you to experiment: run the same task with two or three models, and compare the results.
Why bother with cheap models, if you have Claude? Because cheap changes what you can try. You can run a task on five hundred documents, or run the same task five times, without watching a usage limit. And you learn which of your tasks need the strongest model, and which don’t.






NoteConnecting cheap models through OpenCode Go (click to open)





OpenCode Go is a subscription that bundles a set of open-weights models for $10 a month (November 2026). Kimi K3.1 Pro and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash are both in it.

Subscribe. Go to the OpenCode console, sign in, and subscribe to Go. Then copy your API key. The key is a password for your subscription: don’t share it, and don’t save it in a project folder.
Connect. In OpenCode, type /connect, choose OpenCode Go, and paste your API key.
Choose the model. Type /models and choose DeepSeek V4.1 Flash to start with. You can change it at any time, in the middle of a project too. The list of models changes often, so the names may differ when you read this.

Then test the whole setup:

Read AGENTS.md and tell me in five bullet points what it asks of you. Then create a file called hello-opencode.md with one sentence in it.


It worked if the summary matches your AGENTS.md, and the agent asks for your OK before it creates the file. If it creates the file without asking, the permission setting did not take effect: ask the agent “Where do you read your permission settings from?” and see the permissions documentation.

Limits. Go has a monthly allowance. In any five hours you can use up to a fifth of it, and in any week up to half. If you hit a limit, you wait until it resets.









WarningBefore you put research material into another model



Check where your text goes, as in Step 1.2. With OpenCode Go, each model has its own rules. The OpenCode Go page has a table: how long each model’s provider keeps your text, and which models are offered in exchange for the right to train on what you send. Avoid those for anything that is not public. By default, paid models that train on your data are blocked, and processing is limited to Europe and the United States. Read the table before you start, and note that the list changes. For personal data, the GDPR applies here too.



Four experiments worth running
One task, three models. In a copy of first-project, run Step 2.3 again with the same prompt, once with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and once with Kimi K3.1 Pro, each into its own folder. Then compare them with the extracts Claude made, paper by paper. Do the quotes check out on the page? Is “not stated” used honestly? Is the method described correctly? You will find that the cheapest model is fine for some tasks and not for others. That is worth knowing before you choose a model for a real project.
A large corpus. This is where a cheap model earns its place. Take a few hundred documents: the abstracts of a journal over ten years, speeches from a parliament’s open data, or open-ended answers from a survey of your own. Ask for one row per document.

In data/raw/corpus/ there are several hundred text files. For each file, write one row to data/clean/corpus.csv with: file name, year, main topic (one of the categories in docs/categories.md), and one sentence quoted word for word that supports the topic.
Work in batches of 20 files. After each batch, update status.md with how many files are done. If a file cannot be read or does not fit any category, write "unclear" and go on. Never skip a file silently.
At the end, tell me how many rows you wrote and how many files are in the folder.

Then check it as you would check a research assistant’s coding. Ask for a random sample of 20 rows, read those 20 documents yourself, and count how many rows you agree with. Eighteen out of twenty is a different result from twelve out of twenty, and only the count tells you which one you have.
One task, three runs. A model doesn’t give the same answer every time. With a cheap model you can afford to find out how much that matters. Run the classification above three times, into three files, and ask the agent to list the documents where the three runs disagree. Those are the ambiguous cases, and they are the ones to read yourself.
A cheap worker, a strong reviewer. Let the cheap model do the bulk, such as extracts of two hundred papers. Then switch to a strong model, Kimi K3.1 Pro in OpenCode or Claude in the Claude app, and ask for a review of a sample, as in Step 2.5: “Check 15 randomly chosen extracts against their papers. List anything wrong or unsupported, most serious first.” This is how many research teams work with human assistants, too.
For a more careful way to compare models on your own task, see Choosing a model with evidence in the knowledge base.

title: Part 5: Go Further
text:
What about confidential material?
In Step 1.2 we asked you to keep confidential material out of the folder. There are two ways forward, and neither is a shortcut.
An agreement that covers it. Your university may have a plan or an agreement with a provider that covers such material. This is a question for your data protection officer, not for the agent. See AI and your data.
A model on your own computer. An open-weights model can run on your laptop, so nothing is sent to anyone. It is weaker and slower than the hosted models, and how much weaker depends on the laptop. See Running AI on your own computer. That page is in the knowledge base, and it is more technical than this course.

title: Part 5: Go Further
text:
To read more
In the knowledge base:

Where to run your agent: desktop app, terminal, web or editor.
Open-code tools and Open-weights and local models.
Choosing a model with evidence and Running LLM jobs at scale.







NoteFor the technically curious: the sandbox (click to open)





On Mac and Linux, Claude Code can also enforce the folder boundary through the operating system, so even an approved command can’t write outside the project. This sandbox is off by default and doesn’t run on Windows directly. See the sandboxing documentation if you are curious.




Continue with Part 6: AI in Science →

title: Assignment: Referee the Paper, Improve the Prompt
text:
Assignment · after the session


Referee the Paper, Improve the Prompt


Two tasks on the World Cup project: read what the agent left behind as a referee would, then rewrite the prompt with skills so that the next run is better

title: Assignment: Referee the Paper, Improve the Prompt
text:
What is the assignment?
In Part 3 the agent wrote a paper from a single prompt. The prompt was bare: no rules file, no skills, no review. The assignment has two tasks on that project.



Task
What
Time




A.1
Read the project as a referee would
about two hours


A.2
Improve the prompt with skills
about an hour



The two belong together. In the first task you find what is wrong or unchecked in the paper. In the second you change the prompt so that the agent would catch those things itself.






NoteWhat you will have at the end




Half a page of referee notes on the World Cup paper
Six more skills in your folder, each of which you have read
A rewritten prompt, prompt_v2.md, that uses them



Before you start. Put the project folder we shared into ai-projects, next to first-project. Open it in the Code tab, in Manual mode.

title: Assignment: Referee the Paper, Improve the Prompt
section: A.1 Read the project as a referee would
text:
A.1 Read the project as a referee would
The agent wrote the paper in under an hour, and nobody has checked it. You are the first reader, and you have done the reading: the six papers of Part 2.
Start with a map of the folder:

I am going to referee the paper in this folder. Do not change any files.
Give me a one-page map: which file is the paper, which script made each table and chart, where the raw data is and where it came from, and which files record the choices that were made.

Then go through what the agent left behind. We advise this order. Your agent can help along the way: ask it to explain any file in plain language.

The prompt. Read it again, slowly. What did it specify, and what did it leave open? Everything left open is a choice the agent had to make.
The paper. Read it as a referee. Mark three claims you would question.
The literature. Compare the paper’s main finding with your extracts from Step 2.3. Does it agree with the papers you read? Where it differs, can you see why: other countries, other years, another kind of event, another method?
The decisions memo. Which choices were the agent’s own? Which would you have made differently, and could any of them change the main result? Look for the points that the agent itself marked for review.
The code and the checks. You don’t need to read the code line by line. Read the comment at the top of each script, look at which checks were run, and ask your agent to explain one script.
The slide deck. Compare it with the paper. Does it make the same claims, with the same numbers?
The references. Pick three references and look them up. Does each exist, with these authors, in this journal and year?
One number, traced back. Pick one number from the abstract. Find it in a table, then in the script that made the table, then in the raw data.


You are done when you can write half a page, as a referee would: what the paper claims, how it squares with the literature, what you checked, and what would have to change before you put your name on it.

Save your notes as docs/referee-notes.md in the project folder. You will need them in the next task.

title: Assignment: Referee the Paper, Improve the Prompt
section: A.2 Improve the prompt with skills
text:
A.2 Improve the prompt with skills
Look at your referee notes. Some of what you found is a matter of judgment, and it stays your job. But some of it is routine: verifying the references, comparing the numbers in the text with the tables, rerunning the code. The prompt asked for none of these. A referee should not have to do them. The prompt could have asked.
It could do so in long paragraphs. A skill is the better way: you write the routine down once, and the prompt calls it by name. In Part 2 you used two skills. Here are six more.

Download the skills



Skill
What it does
Based on




new-project
Sets up the project folder, a README and a status note
Scott Cunningham’s /newproject


blindspot
A fresh look at the results before they are interpreted
Scott Cunningham’s /blindspot


referee
Reruns a finished project and files a referee report
Scott Cunningham’s /referee2


ref-check
Checks that every reference exists and is correct
/bibcheck, in our version


paper-check
Finds where a draft contradicts itself or its own tables
our own paper-check


deck
Turns a paper into a slide deck
Scott Cunningham’s /beautiful_deck



All of them, with the two from Part 2, are in one folder on GitHub. The fuller originals by Scott Cunningham are in his MixtapeTools.
One prompt downloads them:

Download these six files exactly (use a download command, do not retype them). Each is called SKILL.md. Save each as .claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md in this folder, where <name> is the folder name in the link.
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/gabors-data-analysis/da-w-ai/main/friendly-agentic-ai-intro/starter/skills/new-project/SKILL.md
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/gabors-data-analysis/da-w-ai/main/friendly-agentic-ai-intro/starter/skills/blindspot/SKILL.md
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/gabors-data-analysis/da-w-ai/main/friendly-agentic-ai-intro/starter/skills/referee/SKILL.md
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/gabors-data-analysis/da-w-ai/main/friendly-agentic-ai-intro/starter/skills/ref-check/SKILL.md
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/gabors-data-analysis/da-w-ai/main/friendly-agentic-ai-intro/starter/skills/paper-check/SKILL.md
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/gabors-data-analysis/da-w-ai/main/friendly-agentic-ai-intro/starter/skills/deck/SKILL.md
Then list the six skills with one line on what each does.


It worked if you start a new session, type /, and the six skills show up in the list.



Read them
Each skill is about a page of plain text, and it is good practice to read a skill before you use it: it is a set of instructions that your agent will follow. Open them in Typora, or on GitHub with the links above.
Every skill starts with a short header between two lines of ---. The name is what you type after /. The description tells the agent when to use the skill on its own. The rest is the recipe.
As you read, keep your referee notes next to you. For each problem you found, ask: is there a skill that would have caught it?


Rewrite the prompt
The original prompt is in the project folder, as initial_prompt.md. Write a new version and save it as prompt_v2.md.

Keep the question and the nine tasks. Change how the tasks are done, not what the paper is about.
Call a skill where it fits, by typing / and its name, as in “Then run /ref-check on the references.” A skill replaces a paragraph of instructions, so the prompt should not get much longer.
Decide the order. When should the fresh look at the results come: before or after the paper is written? Who should run the referee: the session that did the work, or a new one?
Add a stop where you want the agent to wait for you. The original had none.

Write it yourself first. Then ask your agent to comment: “Read initial_prompt.md and prompt_v2.md, and the skills in .claude/skills/. What does my version still leave unchecked? Do not rewrite it.”

You are done when prompt_v2.md calls at least four skills, and for each you can say what it adds that the original prompt did not ask for.







NoteOne possible version (click to open, after you wrote yours)





The about part is unchanged. These are the tasks.
1. Setup: Use /new-project in the current folder.
2. Data: Find fertility across countries. Find football world cup data. Save raw data.
3. Methods: Use well designed econometrics and credible identification strategies. Make sure we think about key mechanism(s). Use /decision-log for every choice. Then show me the design and wait for my OK.
4. Exhibits: Make beautiful graphs and tables as exhibits. When the first results are there, run /blindspot before you write anything, and deal with what it flags.
5. You can use Python or R. Just ensure nice human readable codebase. Install python / R packages when needed.
6. Output1: Write an academic paper. It should be 10-15 pages + references. It should have 8-15 references. Then run /ref-check on the references and /paper-check on the draft, and fix what they find.
7. Output2: Use /deck to turn the paper into slides. Create a PDF slide deck.
8. Review: At the end, hand the folder to a fresh reviewer (a subagent that has not seen the work) and let it run /referee. Keep its report in the folder, and tell me what it found.
9. There may be papers, dissertations, blogposts on this exact task. Disregard them, don't read them, don't cite them at this initial stage.
It is one version among many, and we have not polished it. Note three things. The long description of the decisions memo is gone: /decision-log covers it. There is one stop, after the design. And the referee is a fresh reviewer, because the session that wrote the paper is not its best judge (Step 2.5).





If you want to go on

Run it. Make a new folder, copy prompt_v2.md and the .claude folder into it, and run the prompt. Then compare the new paper with the one we shared. Did the skills change the result, or only how well it is checked? This takes an afternoon and a good part of your usage limit.
Improve a skill. The skills are short on purpose. Each one ends with ideas under Develop it further. Pick the skill that is closest to your own work, and add one check that your field needs.

Both come back in Part 4, where you run a project on a question of your own.

Continue with Part 4: After the Course →

title: Part 4: After the Course
text:
Part 4 of 6 · the weeks after, step by step


After the Course


You are home, with a working agent, referee notes and a better prompt. What to do next, in order: finish what is open, make the rules and the skills yours, and run a project of your own

title: Part 4: After the Course
section: What do we do in this part?
text:
What do we do in this part?
The session is over. You have a working agent, a small project of your own from Part 2, and the World Cup project with its assignment. What should you do with them?
This part is a path through the next few weeks, and it stays with the case study. First you finish what is open. Then you turn what you learned from the World Cup paper into rules and skills of your own. At the end you run the same kind of project on a question from your own field, and review it.
Follow the steps in order. The times are our estimates.



When
Step
Time




The first week
4.1 Finish what is open
about four hours in all


The second week
4.2 Grow your AGENTS.md
half an hour



4.3 Make the skills yours
about an hour



4.4 Keep a history of every change
ten minutes, or an hour with Git


When you have a free afternoon
4.5 Run your prompt on your own question
an afternoon



4.6 Review your own project
about an hour









NoteWhat you will have at the end




A finished first project and a finished assignment
An AGENTS.md with a few rules of your own
One skill you changed, and one you wrote
A first draft on a question from your own field, with a review of it

title: Part 4: After the Course
text:
4.1 Finish what is open
The first week
Two things are open after the session.
Your first project. In class we got as far as Step 2.4. Two steps of Part 2 are left.

Step 2.5: the memo, your review, the revision. Do this one first. A draft, comments on paper, a revision: it is the loop you will use most in your own work.
Step 2.6: a first task with data. This is a separate assignment, on a new question. If you don’t work with data, you may skip it.

Open first-project in the Code tab and start a new session. The agent doesn’t remember the class, so begin with: “Read status.md and tell me where we left off.”
The Assignment. You read the World Cup project as a referee would, and you rewrite its prompt with skills.

You are done when you have docs/memo_v2.docx in first-project, and your referee notes and prompt_v2.md in the World Cup project folder.

title: Part 4: After the Course
text:
4.2 Grow your AGENTS.md
The second week
A skill is a routine you call when you need it. A rule in AGENTS.md holds always. Some of what you found as a referee belongs there.
Open your referee notes from the assignment next to your AGENTS.md. For each problem, ask: would a standing rule have prevented it? Add two or three rules, in your own words. For example:
- Every reference has a DOI or a link that you opened. If you cannot open it, mark the reference as unverified.
- Before you estimate anything, show me the design and wait for my OK.
From here on the rule for growing the file is simple. When the agent makes the same mistake twice, add one line. After a month it will fit how you work better than any template.
When your projects involve data, these lines are worth adding:
- Put checks in the code (row counts, duplicate IDs, merge matches, value ranges, missing values). After each run, save all checks with pass/fail in output/checks.md. If a check fails, stop and tell me.
- Any choice I did not specify goes into DECISIONS.md, marked needs-review.
And keep the file short. A long file is read less carefully, by the agent too. Once a year, ask: “Which lines in AGENTS.md are out of date, or say the same thing twice?”

title: Part 4: After the Course
text:
4.3 Make the skills yours
The second week
The eight skills you have are short on purpose. They are a beginning, and they were written by economists. Now develop them further.
Change one. Pick the skill that is closest to your own work. Each skill ends with ideas under Develop it further. Ask the agent to propose changes, and decide yourself:

Read .claude/skills/referee/SKILL.md. I work in [your field], mostly with [your kind of data or sources]. Propose three additions that a referee in my field would expect. Show me the changes and wait for my OK before you save anything. Keep the skill under two pages.

Then try it: run the changed skill on the World Cup project, and see whether the report got better.
Write one. The best candidates are routines you have repeated two or three times, such as the review loop of Step 2.5. You don’t have to write it yourself. At the end of a session where the routine worked well, ask:

We just went through a routine that worked: reading my comments from a PDF, sorting them into language and content, fixing the language, and asking me about the content one at a time. Write it as a skill in .claude/skills/pdf-comments/SKILL.md, following the format of the read-pdf skill. Keep it under one page.

Then read it, as you would read instructions you give to a new research assistant.
Look at what others wrote. Scott Cunningham’s MixtapeTools has the fuller originals of five of our skills. Anthropic keeps a public collection at github.com/anthropics/skills, and Neal Caren has a set for sociological research (see the useful links). Read a skill before you install it, whoever wrote it: it is a set of instructions that your agent will follow.

You are done when one skill has a check from your own field, and /pdf-comments shows up when you type / in a new session.

title: Part 4: After the Course
section: 4.4 Keep a history of every change
text:
4.4 Keep a history of every change
The second week
In the next step the agent will work for a long time and write many files. Before that, make sure you can go back. There are two ways, a simple one and a precise one.
The simple one: a cloud folder. If your project folder is in Dropbox, OneDrive or Google Drive (Step 1.2), you can already go back in time: each file has a version history. If it is not there yet, move ai-projects there now. For most of us this is enough.
The precise one: version control, usually Git with GitHub. Git keeps a history of your project folder: each commit saves a snapshot of every file, with a one-line note on what changed. GitHub keeps a private copy of that history online. It adds two things. First, you see what changed across sessions and days, line by line. Second, every mistake can be undone by going back to the last version that worked. This makes it cheap to let the agent try things.
The price is about an hour of setup and one habit: commit after each step that works. The agent does most of the typing, and GitHub Desktop shows the history without the terminal. For setup, see Version control with Git and GitHub. For daily use, see Git for working with agents.






TipLet the agent run Git, with you deciding each step (click to open)





Once Git is set up, you can run it entirely through the agent. You read and decide, and the agent does the typing.
1. Review before you commit. Ask for a summary first, and commit only when it matches what you wanted:

Summarize, in plain language, what changed since the last commit: which files, and what changed in each. Propose a one-line commit message. Do not commit yet.

If the summary lists something you didn’t ask for, ask about it before you go on.
2. Commit and push. When the summary is right:

Commit with that message, then push to GitHub.

3. Undo. If a step turns out wrong, even days later:

Revert the last commit, keeping the history. First tell me what this will undo, and wait for my OK.

A revert adds a new commit that undoes an old one, so the record of what happened stays complete. You can also ask about the past: “What changed since Monday, and why?”
If you set up Git, add two lines to AGENTS.md:
- Commit only when I ask. Never push to GitHub without asking.
- Never rewrite or delete Git history.

title: Part 4: After the Course
section: 4.5 Run your prompt on your own question
text:
4.5 Run your prompt on your own question
When you have a free afternoon
Now do what the demo did, on a question you know well. That is the point of choosing your own field: you can judge the result.
Choose the question. It should be one that open data can answer: official statistics, a public survey, a published replication package. Keep confidential data out of it (Step 1.2).
Prepare the folder. Make a new folder in ai-projects. Copy your AGENTS.md and the .claude folder with your skills into it. Put the three or four papers you know best on the question into docs/readings/.
Adapt your prompt. Start from prompt_v2.md, the prompt you wrote in the assignment. Change three things.

The question and the audience. Yours, in one or two sentences, for readers in your field.
The literature. In the demo the agent was told to ignore the literature. Here it should use the papers you gave it, as in Part 2: “The papers in docs/readings/ are the ones I know. Use the read-pdf skill, and cite them with pages.”
The size. A first run can be smaller: 8 to 10 pages, three to five charts and tables.

Keep the stop after the design. The design is the decision that matters most, and it is yours.
Run it. Start in Plan mode and read the plan, as in Step 2.3. For the run itself, Manual mode means a click for every file. The rule of Step 2.1 fits better here: Accept edits, so the agent is free inside the project folder and asks for everything else. Then watch the four things of Part 3: the plan, the choices, the checks and the files.
A long task uses up your usage limit faster than anything in Part 2. If the agent pauses at the limit, nothing is lost: the files are in the folder, and status.md says where the work stands. For the choice of model on long tasks, see Which model should you use?

It worked if the folder has a paper, the scripts that made every number in it, and a DECISIONS.md you can read. It doesn’t have to be a good paper yet.

The first attempt won’t be a paper you can submit. But you will see, on a question you know well, what the agent does well and where it needs you.

title: Part 4: After the Course
text:
4.6 Review your own project
When you have a free afternoon
In Step 2.5 a fresh session reviewed the memo. For a project with data and code, the review goes further: the reviewer reruns everything from scratch. Start a new session and send:

You are reviewing work that someone else did in this folder.
Read AGENTS.md, DECISIONS.md and the scripts in code/.
Rerun all scripts from scratch, in order. Do the outputs match the ones already saved?
Then list anything that looks wrong, untested or undocumented, most serious first. Do not change any files.

This is what the referee skill does, in more steps. If you installed the skills, type /referee in the new session instead, and then /ref-check and /paper-check.
Read the review as you would read a referee report: some points matter, some are noise. Take the serious ones back to the agent, one at a time, each in a new session.
Then be the referee yourself. Go through the eight questions of the Assignment, this time on your own paper. You know this literature and these data better than the agent does, so you will find more than you found in the World Cup paper.
Finally, write down how the work was made: which model, on which date, and what you checked by hand. You will need it when you describe the use of AI in a paper. See Decision logs, reviewing agent work, and disclosing AI use in the knowledge base.

You are done when you can say, for your own draft, what you said for the World Cup paper: what it claims, what you checked, and what would have to change before you put your name on it.

title: Part 4: After the Course
text:
Where are you now?
You have run a project in small steps (Part 2), watched one run from a single prompt (Part 3), refereed it and improved its prompt (the Assignment), and run one of your own with a review (this part). That is the whole routine. From here on it is practice, on your own questions.
Part 5 is different. It has no steps. It is broader advice for the time when the agent is part of your work: other things to use it for, and how to choose your tools.

Continue with Part 5: Go Further →

title: Where to run your agent
text:
Claude Code is one agent, but we can open it in four places: a desktop app, the terminal, a web browser, and a code editor such as VS Code. The model is the same in all four, and so are the instructions it follows. What differs is where the work happens, what we see while it works, and what we need to install. This page helps us choose. It covers Claude Code in detail, and Codex, GitHub Copilot and Google Antigravity briefly, since they come in the same forms.
Checked against official documentation on 22 November 2026. These products change every few months, so check the sources at the end before relying on a detail.
The documentation calls each of these places a surface.

title: Where to run your agent
text:
What is the desktop app?
The Claude app has a Code tab, and that tab is Claude Code with windows and buttons. We type in a prompt box and approve or refuse each step with a click. When the agent changes a file, a diff view shows what was added and removed, line by line. This is the surface the friendly introduction uses, and its Part 1 walks through the installation.
What we need. A paid Claude plan: Pro, Max, Ultra, Team or Enterprise. The app includes Claude Code, so there is nothing else to install and no terminal to open. It runs on macOS (Intel and Apple Silicon) and Windows (x64 and ARM64). On Ubuntu and Debian it is in beta.
What it is good for. Starting out, and any work where we want to see each change before it happens. We can run several sessions side by side, and there is an optional terminal pane for the rare moment we want one. The same app can also start a session in the cloud: in the environment selector, Local means our computer, Cloud means a machine run by Anthropic.
Limits. Console credits are not enough here: the app needs a subscription. And we can’t run the app from a script; for that we need the terminal version.

title: Where to run your agent
text:
What is the terminal version?
Here Claude Code is a command. We open a terminal, move to the project folder and type claude. The conversation happens in the terminal window, as text. The documentation calls it the full-featured version.
What we need. A paid Claude plan, or a Claude Console account with prepaid credits (the Console is Anthropic’s pay-per-use account for developers; see How to get an API key). It installs with one command on Mac, Windows and Linux: see Installing AI CLI tools. On Windows, the documentation recommends installing Git for Windows as well. We also need some comfort with the command line: moving between folders, reading an error message. If that is new, read Terminal basics first.
What it is good for. Three things the other surfaces do less well. First, it has every command; the editor extension has only a subset. Second, it can be scripted: claude -p "..." runs one instruction and exits, so it fits into a script or a pipeline. Third, it runs on Linux, so it also runs on a server we log into, such as a university computing cluster, next to data that is too large to copy to a laptop.
Limits. Changes are shown as text, not in a diff window, which takes some getting used to. When we want the visual view, typing /desktop moves the current session into the desktop app (on macOS and x64 Windows, with a Claude subscription).

title: Where to run your agent
text:
What is the editor version?
Claude Code also comes as an extension for VS Code and as a plugin for JetBrains editors such as PyCharm and IntelliJ IDEA. It opens in a panel next to our code files. In VS Code, a proposed change appears as a side-by-side comparison that we accept or reject, and a plan opens as a Markdown document we can comment on before the agent starts.
What we need. A paid Claude plan or a Console account. VS Code 1.94 or later. The VS Code extension brings what its panel needs, but to type claude in VS Code’s own terminal we install the terminal version too. The same extension installs in Cursor. The JetBrains plugin needs the terminal version installed separately. In an editor without an extension, such as RStudio, we can run the terminal version in the editor’s terminal.
What it is good for. Work where we read and write code ourselves, next to the agent: we see the script, the agent’s change to it and the output in one window. For setting up VS Code with Python or R, see VS Code setup.
Limits. Not every command of the terminal version is in the extension. The documentation suggests running claude in the editor’s terminal for the missing ones.

title: Where to run your agent
section: What is the web version, and what runs in the cloud?
text:
What is the web version, and what runs in the cloud?
At claude.ai/code, or in the Code tab of the Claude mobile app, Claude Code runs in a cloud session. The work does not happen on our computer. It happens on a virtual machine that Anthropic manages. The machine copies our project from GitHub, works on that copy, and sends its changes back to GitHub on a separate branch (see Git for agents). We review them and, if we like them, open a pull request: a proposal to merge the branch into the main version.
What we need. A Pro, Max, Ultra or Team plan, or an Enterprise seat that includes Claude Code. A GitHub account connected to Claude, and the project in a GitHub repository. Nothing to install. Cloud sessions count toward the plan’s usage limits, with no separate charge for the machine.
What it is good for. Long tasks we want to start and check on later: the session keeps running when we close the laptop. Several tasks at once, each in its own session. And work from a phone or a borrowed computer.
Limits. The cloud machine sees only what is in the repository. It can’t see the files on our laptop, our Dropbox folder, or data we keep out of git. Its internet access is limited by default. Cloning and pull requests work with GitHub; other hosts work only partly. A session that sits idle for a while stops, and reopening it starts a fresh machine with the conversation restored.
We can move work between cloud and local. From the terminal, claude --cloud "task" starts a cloud session on the current repository (push local commits first, since the cloud clones from GitHub), and claude --teleport pulls a cloud session back into the terminal. The desktop app can send a local session to the cloud from its Open in menu.
