title: Where to run your agent
section: Does our setup carry over between surfaces?
text:
Does our setup carry over between surfaces?
Mostly, yes. Say we start a project in the desktop app, and a month later we open the same folder in the terminal. The agent finds the same files, and it reads the same instructions: Claude Code reads the project’s CLAUDE.md on every surface. If the project has an AGENTS.md and no CLAUDE.md, Claude Code reads AGENTS.md instead. Codex reads AGENTS.md too, and the Antigravity CLI reads both AGENTS.md and GEMINI.md. Skills in the project’s .claude/skills/ folder come along with the folder, and personal skills in ~/.claude/skills/ work in both the desktop app and the terminal.
It is good practice to keep the instructions in the project folder, not in our heads or in a chat history. Then switching surfaces, or switching agents, costs almost nothing.
There is one exception. A cloud session sees only what is committed to the repository and pushed to GitHub. An instructions file that lives only on our laptop doesn’t reach it. So commit CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md and push it. For a gentle start with git, see Git for agents.

title: Where to run your agent
text:
Which one should we use?
In this course, we start with the desktop app. It needs no terminal, it shows every change before it happens, and the friendly introduction is built around it.
Later, once we write code ourselves, the editor version is the natural next step: the agent works in the same window as our scripts. The terminal version is worth learning when we want to script the agent or run it on a server. Nothing is lost by moving, since the project folder and its instructions come along.
We use the cloud for repositories that hold no confidential data: a public replication package, course material, a package we develop. It is the best surface for long tasks we don’t want to watch. It needs GitHub, but most code projects belong there anyway.






WarningCloud sessions and confidential data



On every surface, the agent sends what it reads to Anthropic’s servers, as Part 1 of the friendly introduction explains. The local surfaces at least keep our files on our computer. A cloud session goes further: it puts a copy of the whole repository on a remote machine, and its changes are pushed to GitHub. So keep interview transcripts, identifiable survey data and anything under a data-use agreement out of any repository we use with cloud sessions, even a private one. Check the data agreement before using any surface with such material. For what providers keep and what the GDPR asks, see AI and your data. For data that must not leave the computer at all, see Running AI on your own computer.

title: Walkthrough: Using soccerdata to Fetch Arsenal’s 2023–24 Match Stats
text:
Below is a simple, step-by-step recipe for pulling Arsenal’s match-by-match team statistics for the 2023–24 Premier League season from FBref, using the soccerdata Python client library. You never write raw HTTP requests—soccerdata handles those for you.
Note (2026): FBref has no official API. soccerdata downloads and parses FBref’s web pages, and because FBref now blocks bots it drives a real browser and waits between requests. Since January 2026 FBref no longer shows Opta’s advanced stats (xG, progressive passes, shot-creating actions); results, tables and basic stats remain.

title: Walkthrough: Using soccerdata to Fetch Arsenal’s 2023–24 Match Stats
text:
R equivalent
# 1. Install and load the package
install.packages("worldfootballR")  # different package, same idea
library(worldfootballR)

# 2. Get Arsenal match results from the Premier League 2023/24
arsenal_matches <- fb_team_match_results(
  team_url = "https://fbref.com/en/squads/18bb7c10/2023-2024/Arsenal-Stats")

# 3. Inspect the data
head(arsenal_matches)

title: Terminal Basics
text:
A terminal (also called command line, shell, or console) is a text-based interface to your computer. Instead of clicking icons, you type commands.
Why does this matter for Claude Code? The terminal version of Claude Code runs there (the desktop app does not need the terminal). It reads your files, runs code, and shows results - all through text commands.
Don’t worry: You don’t need to become a terminal expert. Just learn the basics below.

title: Running AI on your own computer
text:
An open-weights model can run on your own computer. Then nothing is sent to a company’s servers, and the model works with the Wi-Fi switched off. This page shows how to set it up, and what to expect from it. For the background on open-weights models, see Open-weights and local models.
Why would we want this? There are three reasons.
True, it has a price. A model that fits on a laptop is weaker and slower than the hosted models. How much weaker depends on the laptop, and this is why we separate two use cases.

title: Running AI on your own computer
section: What decides what you can run?
text:
What decides what you can run?
Three things matter, and they compete for the same memory.
Memory. The model has to fit into memory that the graphics processor can use. On a Mac with Apple silicon, this is the ordinary memory of the computer, which is why Macs with a lot of memory are popular for this. On a Windows or Linux laptop, it is the memory of the graphics card, which is often only 8 to 16 GB even on an expensive machine. If the model doesn’t fit, part of it runs on the main processor, and it gets much slower. As a rule of thumb from practice, plan for the size of the model file plus several gigabytes.
Model size. A model’s size is given in billions of parameters, such as 8b or 30b. Larger models are better and need more memory. The files you download are compressed versions (quantized, usually to four bits per parameter), which costs a little quality and saves a lot of memory.
Context length. This is how much text the model can see at once, measured in tokens (a token is about three quarters of a word). A long context needs extra memory on top of the model. An agent needs a long one: the OpenCode documentation asks for at least 64,000 tokens. Ollama’s default is much shorter, so we have to raise it.

title: Running AI on your own computer
text:
Setup, for both use cases
We use Ollama, a free program that downloads open-weights models and runs them. It works on Windows, Mac and Linux.
1. Install Ollama, from ollama.com/download.
2. Download a model. In a terminal:
ollama pull qwen3:8b
Which model? See the two use cases below. Choose one marked tools in the Ollama library: an agent can’t work without that.
3. Raise the context length. In the Ollama app, open Settings and set the context length to 64k. Or set it when starting Ollama from a terminal:
OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=64000 ollama serve
On Windows, quit Ollama first, set OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH under Edit environment variables for your account, and start Ollama again.
4. Switch off the cloud. Ollama also offers models that run on its own servers. Their names end in :cloud or -cloud. For confidential material, rule them out: set the environment variable OLLAMA_NO_CLOUD=1, or add "disable_ollama_cloud": true to the file ~/.ollama/server.json, and restart Ollama.
5. Check that the model fits. Start a chat with ollama run qwen3:8b, ask something, and in a second terminal type:
ollama ps
The PROCESSOR column should say 100% GPU. A split such as 48%/52% CPU/GPU means the model doesn’t fit into the graphics memory. It will work, but slowly. Choose a smaller model or a shorter context.
6. Test it offline. Switch off the Wi-Fi and ask the model a question. If it answers, the model is on your computer, and your text stays there.

title: Running AI on your own computer
section: Use case 1: a good model on a top laptop
text:
Use case 1: a good model on a top laptop
With 64 to 128 GB of memory that the model can use, we can run models that are good enough for real agent work. They are behind the best hosted models, but they can plan a task of several steps, call tools, and work through a folder of documents.

Use it as an agent. OpenCode is an open-source agent application that works with local models. With Ollama running, one command starts it with a local model:
ollama launch opencode
Or start OpenCode as usual, type /models, and choose the local model listed under Ollama. Your AGENTS.md and your skills work as they are. For the setup of OpenCode and its permission settings, see Part 5 of the friendly introduction.
What should we expect? The agent is slower than a hosted one, and the fan will run. It makes more mistakes on long tasks, so keep the steps small: one paper, one script, one table at a time. And keep the checks of Part 2: quotes found on the page, a random sample read by hand.

title: Running AI on your own computer
section: Use case 2: a simple model on an ordinary laptop
text:
Use case 2: a simple model on an ordinary laptop
With 16 to 32 GB of memory, we can run small models. They are not good agents: with a 64k context they are slow, and they lose the thread on tasks of many steps. But they do one narrow thing per document quite well, and for confidential text that is often all we need.



Model
Download
Context
Memory to plan for




qwen3:4b
2.5 GB
256K
8 GB or more


qwen3:8b
5.2 GB
40K
16 GB

256K
16 GB


gemma4:e4b
6.6–9.5 GB
128K

gpt-oss:20b
14 GB
128K
24–32 GB



Use it from a script, in batches. The reliable way to use a small model is not as an agent. A short script sends one document at a time with the same instruction, and writes one row per document. Then each call is short, a long context is not needed, and a failure affects one row only.
Ollama speaks the same API as the hosted models, at http://localhost:11434/v1. So a script written for a hosted model needs two changes: the address and the model name.
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="http://localhost:11434/v1", api_key="ollama")  # the key is not checked

answer = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="qwen3:8b",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "Classify the answer into one of: work, family, health, other. Reply with the category only."},
        {"role": "user", "content": "I had to stop working when my mother got ill."},
    ],
    temperature=0,
)
print(answer.choices[0].message.content)
You don’t have to write this yourself. Ask your usual agent, which may be a hosted one, to write the script, and show it only made-up examples. Then run the script yourself, on the real data, with the local model. The confidential text never leaves the laptop. For the basics of such scripts, see LLM APIs in Python.
Three tasks that suit a small local model:

Coding open-ended answers into a fixed set of categories, with the words that justify the choice quoted exactly.
Pulling a few facts out of each document: a date, a place, an amount, yes or no.
Replacing names with codes ([PERSON_1], [PLACE_2]), with the list of replacements saved in a separate key file.

For each, check a random sample of 20 rows by hand, as you would with a human coder. Run the script a second time and look at the rows where the two runs disagree.






WarningLocal is not the same as allowed



A local model solves one problem: your material is not sent to a company. Your other duties stay as they were: what participants consented to, where the files may be stored, who may see them. Replacing names with codes is not anonymisation in the sense of the GDPR: as long as the key file exists, or a person can be recognized from the context, the text is still personal data. When in doubt, ask your data protection officer.

title: Running AI on your own computer
text:
Other tools

LM Studio does the same job as Ollama, with windows and buttons and a model browser. Its local address is http://127.0.0.1:1234/v1, and OpenCode can use it too.
Hosted open-weights models are the middle way when the laptop is too small and the material is not confidential. See Part 5 of the friendly introduction.

title: How to Generate a PDF Report
text: There are several ways to turn your analysis into a polished PDF report. Which option works best depends on what software you already have installed. This guide covers six approaches, from the most feature-rich to the most minimal.

title: How to Generate a PDF Report
text: There are several ways to turn your analysis into a polished PDF report. Which option works best depends on what software you already have installed. This guide covers six approaches, from the most feature-rich to the most minimal.

title: How to Generate a PDF Report
text:
Option 1: Quarto (recommended if available)
Requires: Quarto (plus R or Python only if your .qmd executes those languages); pandoc is bundled with Quarto.
Quarto is the modern standard. It ships with pandoc, so no separate install is needed. You write code and narrative together in a .qmd file, and Quarto handles execution and typesetting.
Install:
# Windows (winget)
winget install --id Posit.Quarto --source winget --exact

# macOS (Homebrew)
brew install --cask quarto

# Or download from https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/
Verify setup:
quarto --version
quarto check
For PDF output, you also need LaTeX. The easiest route is TinyTeX:
quarto install tinytex
Render:
quarto render report.qmd              # uses format specified in YAML
quarto render report.qmd --to pdf     # force PDF output
quarto render report.qmd --to html    # HTML fallback (no LaTeX needed)
Tip: Quarto 1.4+ supports format: typst, which bundles its own typesetting engine and does not need LaTeX at all:
---
title: "My Report"
format: typst
---

title: How to Generate a PDF Report
text:
Option 2: R Markdown
Requires: R + rmarkdown package + pandoc + LaTeX
The predecessor to Quarto. Uses .Rmd files with R code chunks. Very mature ecosystem with many templates.
If you do not use RStudio or Quarto, install pandoc separately (see Option 4).
Install:
# In R console
install.packages("rmarkdown")

# For LaTeX (minimal distribution, ~250 MB)
install.packages("tinytex")
tinytex::install_tinytex()
Verify setup:
rmarkdown::find_pandoc()
tinytex::is_tinytex()
Render:
rmarkdown::render("report.Rmd", output_format = "pdf_document")
rmarkdown::render("report.Rmd", output_format = "html_document")  # no LaTeX needed

title: How to Generate a PDF Report
text:
Option 3: Python + LaTeX
Requires: Python (pandas, matplotlib) + xelatex or pdflatex
Python generates figures as PNGs and writes a .tex file. A LaTeX engine compiles it to PDF. This gives you full control over layout.
Install:
# Python packages
pip install pandas matplotlib numpy

# LaTeX -- pick one:
# Windows: MiKTeX (smaller/easier) or TeX Live
# https://miktex.org/download
# https://tug.org/texlive/
# macOS:
brew install --cask basictex     # minimal (~100 MB)
brew install --cask mactex       # full (~5 GB)
# Or use TinyTeX via R (see Option 2)
Verify setup:
xelatex --version   # or: pdflatex --version
Run:
python report.py
# Typical flow: your script writes report.tex, then you compile with xelatex
Manual compilation (if needed):
xelatex report.tex    # run twice for table of contents
xelatex report.tex

title: How to Generate a PDF Report
text:
Option 4: Python + pandoc
Requires: Python (pandas, matplotlib) + pandoc + LaTeX
Python generates figures, you write the narrative in plain Markdown, and pandoc converts everything to PDF. Easier than writing raw LaTeX.
Install:
# Python packages
pip install pandas matplotlib numpy

# pandoc
# Windows:
winget install --source winget --exact --id JohnMacFarlane.Pandoc
# macOS:
brew install pandoc

# You still need LaTeX for PDF output (see Option 3)
Verify setup:
pandoc --version
Run:
# First generate your figures
python generate_figures.py

# Then convert Markdown to PDF
pandoc report.md -o report.pdf --pdf-engine=xelatex

# Or to HTML (no LaTeX needed)
pandoc report.md -o report.html --standalone

title: How to Generate a PDF Report
text:
Option 5: Jupyter Notebook export
Requires: Python + Jupyter + nbconvert + pandoc + LaTeX (for PDF)
Write code and narrative together in .ipynb notebook cells, then export.
Install:
pip install jupyter nbconvert
# For PDF export, also install:
# - pandoc (see Option 4)
# - LaTeX (see Option 3)
Export:
jupyter nbconvert --to pdf notebook.ipynb     # needs pandoc + LaTeX
jupyter nbconvert --to html notebook.ipynb    # no LaTeX needed
Notebook UIs also offer Export/Download-as-PDF actions, but menu labels vary by app/version.

title: How to Generate a PDF Report
text:
Option 6: Python + fpdf2 (no LaTeX needed)
Requires: Python 3.11+ (pandas, matplotlib, fpdf2)
A pure-Python option that produces text and figures in a PDF without any LaTeX or pandoc install. Limited typographic control but zero external dependencies.
Install:
pip install pandas matplotlib fpdf2
Verify setup:
python -c "from fpdf import FPDF; print('fpdf2 ok')"
Example:
from fpdf import FPDF

pdf = FPDF()
pdf.set_auto_page_break(auto=True, margin=15)

# Title page
pdf.add_page()
pdf.set_font("Helvetica", "B", 24)
pdf.cell(w=0, h=20, text="My Report Title", new_x="LMARGIN", new_y="NEXT", align="C")

# Section with text
pdf.set_font("Helvetica", "B", 14)
pdf.cell(w=0, h=12, text="1. Introduction", new_x="LMARGIN", new_y="NEXT")
pdf.set_font("Helvetica", size=11)
pdf.multi_cell(w=0, h=6, text="Your narrative text goes here...")

# Insert a figure
pdf.image("exhibits/fig1.png", w=170)

pdf.output("report.pdf")

Yes

title: How to Generate a PDF Report
text:
Which should I pick?

Already have Quarto? Use Option 1. It’s the simplest end-to-end workflow.
Already have R? Use Option 2. Install tinytex for LaTeX and you’re set.
Only have Python + LaTeX? Use Option 3.
Have Python but no LaTeX? Use Option 6 (fpdf2) for a quick PDF, or Option 4/5 with --to html as a fallback.
Want to avoid installing anything heavy? Use Quarto with format: typst (Option 1) or fpdf2 (Option 6) — neither needs LaTeX.

title: Open-code tools
text: This course uses two harnesses: Claude Code and VS Code + GitHub Copilot. Both are commercial products tied to a provider. There is a third category worth knowing about: open-source coding agents — “open-code” tools — that you run yourself and point at whatever model you like.

title: Open-code tools
text:
What “harness” means here
A harness is the program that wraps a language model and lets it actually do things: read your files, run code, edit files, call tools, and loop until a task is done. The model is the engine; the harness is the car. The harness matters as much as the model — a great model in a clumsy harness is frustrating, and a good harness makes a mid-tier model genuinely useful.

title: Open-code tools
section: Open-code tools vs the two we use
text:
Open-code tools vs the two we use









Claude Code / Copilot
Open-code tools




Source
Closed, vendor-built
Open-source, community or vendor-released


Model
Tied to a provider (Anthropic / your Copilot model)
Bring your own — frontier API or local open-weights


Setup
Sign in, go
Install + configure + supply a key/endpoint


Why pick it
Polished, supported, low-friction
Flexibility, transparency, run fully local



Examples in this space include open-source CLI agents and editor extensions that accept any model endpoint (including a local Ollama server). The landscape moves fast, so treat specific names as examples, not endorsements.

title: Open-code tools
section: Why it matters for this course
text:
Why it matters for this course
The point is conceptual transfer, not a third tool to learn:

Everything you learn in Claude Code — give the agent context, let it run and verify, inspect the diff, iterate — transfers directly to any open-code harness.
Open-code tools are the bridge between the open-weights models page and real work: they’re how you put a local, private, reproducible model into an agentic workflow.
If you ever need a fully local, private agentic setup (sensitive data, air-gapped, no per-token cost), an open-code tool pointed at a local model is the way to get it.







Note



We do not require you to install an open-code tool. It’s a stretch/awareness topic: know the category exists, understand it’s the same workflow with a swappable engine, and reach for it when privacy or cost rules out the commercial harnesses.

title: Running LLM jobs at scale
text:
Prices and API details checked on 22 November 2026.
Say we have 20,000 open-ended survey answers, and we want each one coded into one of twelve categories. Calling LLM APIs from Python showed how to classify one text, then ten. This page is the next step: running the same call 20,000 times at a cost we know in advance, and keeping every result. The order of work we suggest is this: estimate the cost, run a pilot, then run the full job as a batch, with caching and a log.

title: Running LLM jobs at scale
section: How much will the job cost?
text:
How much will the job cost?
The arithmetic is simple. Cost = documents × (input tokens per document × input price + output tokens per document × output price). Prices are quoted per million tokens.
Input tokens per document are the instructions (the codebook) plus the text itself. Output tokens are the answer plus the model’s thinking. Note that the current small models think before answering by default, and the thinking is billed as output tokens even when we never see it. Lowering the effort setting cuts it.
Don’t guess the input length, count it. Anthropic’s token counting endpoint is free:
import anthropic

# CODEBOOK: the codebook as one string; df: a data frame with columns id and text
client = anthropic.Anthropic()
n = client.messages.count_tokens(
    model="claude-haiku-5-5",
    system=CODEBOOK,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": df["text"].iloc[0]}],
)
print(n.input_tokens)
Let’s work through the example. The codebook is 1,500 tokens, an average answer is 150 tokens, and we assume 100 output tokens per answer. Over 20,000 answers, that is 33 million input tokens and 2 million output tokens.










Model
Price per million tokens (input / output)
Standard
Batch
Standard, codebook cached




claude-haiku-5-5
$0.10 / $0.50
$4.30
$2.15
$1.60


gpt-6-luna
$0.10 / $0.50
$4.30
$2.15
about $1.60


claude-sonnet-5-5
$2 / $10
$86
$43
$29


claude-opus-5-5
$4 / $20
$172
$86
$58



Two things stand out. The large model costs 40 times as much as the small one for the same job. And the two discounts, batch and caching, cut the bill by half and by about two thirds. They can also be combined. The weakest number in the table is the 100 output tokens, because thinking varies by task. The pilot replaces it with a measured one.

title: Running LLM jobs at scale
section: Why start with a pilot of 50 to 100 documents?
text:
Why start with a pilot of 50 to 100 documents?
A pilot tells us two things before we spend real money: whether the labels are right, and what a document actually costs.
It is good practice to draw a random sample of 100 documents and code them ourselves before looking at any model output. Then we run the model on the same 100, compare the two sets of labels, and read every disagreement. Most disagreements point to a vague category in the codebook. We fix the wording and rerun on the same 100. When we are happy, we check the final codebook on 50 fresh documents that played no role in the tuning, as we would hold out a test sample.
The pilot also gives us measured tokens. Every response reports usage.input_tokens and usage.output_tokens, so we can redo the cost estimate with real averages. The whole pilot costs a few cents. This is also the moment to compare a small and a large model on the same 100 documents, as described in Choosing a model with evidence.

title: Running LLM jobs at scale
section: What is a batch API, and when should we use it?
text:
What is a batch API, and when should we use it?
A batch API takes all our requests in one go, processes them when the provider has spare capacity, and returns the results later at half the price. No one waits for 20,000 survey codes in real time, so for this kind of job the batch is the natural default.









Anthropic Message Batches
OpenAI Batch API




Discount
50%
50%


Turnaround
Most within 1 hour, at most 24 hours
Within 24 hours, often faster


Size limit
100,000 requests or 256 MB
50,000 requests, 200 MB input file


Results kept
29 days
30 days by default



Results may come back in a different order than we sent them, so each request carries a custom_id and we match on it. With Anthropic, we send a list of requests and keep the batch ID:
from anthropic.types.message_create_params import MessageCreateParamsNonStreaming
from anthropic.types.messages.batch_create_params import Request

requests = [
    Request(
        custom_id=f"r{row.id}",
        params=MessageCreateParamsNonStreaming(
            model="claude-haiku-5-5",
            max_tokens=1024,                    # thinking counts toward this
            output_config={"effort": "low"},
            system=[{"type": "text", "text": CODEBOOK,
                     "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral", "ttl": "1h"}}],
            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": row.text}],
        ),
    )
    for row in df.itertuples()
]
batch = client.messages.batches.create(requests=requests)
open("batch_id.txt", "w").write(batch.id)  # needed to collect the results later
Later, maybe after lunch, we collect the results:
import pandas as pd
batch_id = open("batch_id.txt").read()
batch = client.messages.batches.retrieve(batch_id)
if batch.processing_status == "ended":
    rows = []
    for r in client.messages.batches.results(batch_id):
        if r.result.type == "succeeded":
            msg = r.result.message
            text = next((b.text for b in msg.content if b.type == "text"), "")
            rows.append({"custom_id": r.custom_id, "label": text.strip(), "model": msg.model})
        else:  # errored, canceled or expired: send these again
            rows.append({"custom_id": r.custom_id, "label": None, "status": r.result.type})
    pd.DataFrame(rows).to_csv("batch_results.csv", index=False)
With OpenAI, we write the requests to a JSONL file (plain text, one request per line), upload it, and point the batch at the Responses endpoint:
import json
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI()
with open("batch_input.jsonl", "w") as f:
    for row in df.itertuples():
        f.write(json.dumps({"custom_id": f"r{row.id}", "method": "POST", "url": "/v1/responses",
                            "body": {"model": "gpt-6-luna", "instructions": CODEBOOK,
                                     "input": row.text, "reasoning": {"effort": "low"}}}) + "\n")

batch_file = client.files.create(file=open("batch_input.jsonl", "rb"), purpose="batch")
batch = client.batches.create(input_file_id=batch_file.id, endpoint="/v1/responses",
                              completion_window="24h")
open("batch_id_openai.txt", "w").write(batch.id)  # needed to collect the results later

# later, also in a new session
import pandas as pd
batch = client.batches.retrieve(open("batch_id_openai.txt").read())
if batch.status == "completed":
    results = []
    for line in client.files.content(batch.output_file_id).text.splitlines():
        r = json.loads(line)
        body = r["response"]["body"]
        text = next(c["text"] for item in body["output"] if item["type"] == "message"
                    for c in item["content"] if c["type"] == "output_text")
        results.append({"custom_id": r["custom_id"], "label": text.strip()})
    pd.DataFrame(results).to_csv("batch_results.csv", index=False)
Failed requests go to a separate file, found through batch.error_file_id.

title: Running LLM jobs at scale
section: How does prompt caching cut the cost of a long codebook?
text:
How does prompt caching cut the cost of a long codebook?
Every one of our 20,000 requests starts with the same 1,500-token codebook. With prompt caching, the provider keeps that processed beginning for a while, and the next request that starts with exactly the same text reads it from the cache at a fraction of the input price. The rule that follows: fixed text first, the document last.
With Anthropic we mark the end of the fixed part with cache_control, as in the batch code above. A cache read costs 0.1 times the base input price on Claude Haiku 5.5, and 0.05 times on Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Opus 5.5. Writing to the cache costs 1.25 times the base price for the default 5-minute lifetime, and 2 times for the 1-hour option. The current models cache prompts of 512 tokens or more. A shorter prompt is simply not cached, with no error. Inside a batch, cache hits are best effort, and the documentation suggests the 1-hour cache there. Check usage.cache_read_input_tokens in the pilot: if it stays at zero, the cache is not working.
With OpenAI, caching is automatic for prompts of at least 1,024 tokens on recent models, cached input costs 0.1 times the normal rate on most models, and usage.input_tokens_details.cached_tokens shows what was read from the cache.

title: Running LLM jobs at scale
section: What happens when we hit a rate limit?
text:
What happens when we hit a rate limit?
Providers cap how much we can send per minute: requests, input tokens and output tokens. Above the cap, the API returns error 429. Both Python packages, anthropic and openai, retry such errors automatically, twice by default, with growing pauses. For a long loop we can raise this with anthropic.Anthropic(max_retries=5) or OpenAI(max_retries=5). With Anthropic, tokens read from the cache don’t count toward the input-token limit. A sudden jump in traffic can also trigger a 429, so start a big loop slowly rather than all at once.
Batch jobs have their own, separate limits, which is one more reason to prefer them for large jobs. Note that not every error is worth retrying. A 400 means the request itself is wrong, and a 429 that says the monthly spend cap is reached will keep failing until the cap is raised or the next month starts.

title: Running LLM jobs at scale
section: How do we make sure a crash doesn’t lose work?
text:
How do we make sure a crash doesn’t lose work?
When we run requests one by one, each result should go to disk the moment it arrives, one line per document. If the script stops after 12,000 documents, because of a dropped connection or a laptop lid, we restart it, it reads the file, and it skips what is done.
import anthropic, datetime, hashlib, json, os

client = anthropic.Anthropic(max_retries=5)
PROMPT_VERSION = hashlib.sha256(CODEBOOK.encode()).hexdigest()[:8]
OUT = "labels.jsonl"

done = set()
if os.path.exists(OUT):
    with open(OUT) as f:
        done = {json.loads(line)["id"] for line in f}

with open(OUT, "a") as f:
    for row in df.itertuples():
        if row.id in done:
            continue
        msg = client.messages.create(
            model="claude-haiku-5-5", max_tokens=1024, output_config={"effort": "low"},
            system=[{"type": "text", "text": CODEBOOK, "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}}],
            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": row.text}],
        )
        f.write(json.dumps({
            "id": row.id,
            "label": next((b.text for b in msg.content if b.type == "text"), "").strip(),
            "stop_reason": msg.stop_reason,          # "max_tokens" means the answer was cut off
            "model": msg.model, "prompt_version": PROMPT_VERSION,
            "date": datetime.date.today().isoformat(),
            "input_tokens": msg.usage.input_tokens,
            "cache_read_tokens": msg.usage.cache_read_input_tokens,
            "output_tokens": msg.usage.output_tokens,
        }) + "\n")
        f.flush()
For a batch, the equivalent is to save the batch ID to a file right after creating it. The results wait on the provider’s side for about a month.

title: Running LLM jobs at scale
section: How do we keep the results reproducible?
text:
How do we keep the results reproducible?
Each row in the file above carries the exact model ID returned by the API, the date, and a prompt version. The version is a short hash of the codebook text, so any change to the wording gives a new version. Keep the codebook in its own file under git, next to the script.
Why bother? Hosted models are retired. OpenAI’s gpt-4o-mini shuts down on 14 January 2027, with gpt-6-luna as the suggested replacement. A referee who asks for a rerun in two years may get a different model, and the log is what tells us which model produced the numbers in the paper. If exact reruns matter, a downloaded local model is the safer choice. See Reproducible research for the wider workflow.

title: Running LLM jobs at scale
section: How do we stop a runaway bill?
text:
How do we stop a runaway bill?
Set a spend limit before the full run, not after. In the Claude Console, under Spend limits, we can set a monthly limit below our tier’s cap. Above it, requests fail with an error instead of costing money. We can also give the project its own workspace with its own limit. OpenAI offers a spend alert, which only sends a notification, and a hard spend limit, which stops requests, for the whole organization or for one project.
Also watch the first thousand documents. If the tokens per document are far above the pilot’s numbers, stop and find out why.

title: Running LLM jobs at scale
section: When is a cheap model or a local model the better choice?
text:
When is a cheap model or a local model the better choice?
For classification into fixed categories, or for pulling a few fields out of each text, a small model is usually enough. Anthropic itself positions Claude Haiku 5.5 for high-volume work such as classification and extraction. A larger model earns its price when the categories need judgment, when the documents are long and subtle, or when the pilot shows clear errors that a better prompt doesn’t fix. We decide on the pilot numbers.
A local model is the better choice when the texts are confidential, when exact reruns matter, or when there is no budget for a per-token bill. The price is time: a laptop is much slower than a hosted model. The script barely changes, and checkpointing matters even more for runs that take a whole night. See Running AI on your own computer.

title: Running LLM jobs at scale
text:
What about R?
The ellmer package has batch_chat(), which sends prompts through the batch APIs of OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini and Groq. It saves the state of the job in a JSON file, so we can stop R and rerun the same line later to pick up the results. batch_chat_text() returns the answers as a character vector, and batch_chat_structured() returns structured data, by default as a data frame. The package marks these functions as experimental. For requests that should come back right away, parallel_chat() sends several at a time.
library(ellmer)
chat <- chat_anthropic(model = "claude-haiku-5-5", system_prompt = codebook)
labels <- batch_chat_text(chat = chat, prompts = as.list(df$text), path = "labels-batch.json")

text:

title: Knowledge Bases for Agents
text:
A README is written for a person reading top to bottom. An AI agent works differently: it lands in your project cold, needs to find the one table relevant to the question, and wants to load only that — not your entire 400-line data description. As we hand more of our analysis to agentic tools like Claude Code, the way we document data starts to matter for machines as much as for humans.
The good news: the same plain-markdown habits that make documentation good for people also make it navigable for agents — if you add a little structure. This page introduces metadata as code and a lightweight convention built on it, the Open Knowledge Format (OKF).
This builds directly on Documentation Fundamentals — read that first if you haven’t.

title: Knowledge Bases for Agents
text:
Metadata as Code
“Metadata as code” means your documentation about the data lives in the repository, in plain text, under version control — right next to the code and data it describes. Not in a separate wiki, not in a vendor’s catalog UI, not in a shared drive that drifts out of date.
The benefits mirror those of code itself:







Property
What you get




Version controlled
Documentation changes are tracked in git alongside data changes


Diffable
You can see exactly what changed in a table description and when


Portable
Move the repo, the knowledge comes with it — no lock-in


Readable by both
Same file serves a human (renders nicely) and an agent (parses cleanly)

title: Knowledge Bases for Agents
text:
The Open Knowledge Format
OKF is an open, vendor-neutral convention first published by Google Cloud in 2026 (now at version 0.3, in its own repository). Strip away the cloud framing and the core is deliberately tiny:

A directory of markdown files, one per “concept” — a table, a dataset, a metric. The file path is the concept’s name.
Each file opens with YAML frontmatter: a small block of structured fields. Only type: is required; everything else is optional but queryable.
Concepts link to each other with ordinary markdown links, forming a knowledge graph richer than the folder tree.
Optional index.md files let an agent navigate in progressively, and log.md files record change history.

That’s it. No SDK, no database, no runtime. It works with the text editor, git, and AI tools you already use. The bet — voiced by Andrej Karpathy — is that the tedious cross-reference bookkeeping that makes humans abandon wikis is exactly what LLMs do tirelessly.

What a concept file looks like
Here is a single table from a football dataset, documented OKF-style:
---
type: Table
title: matches
description: One row per match — the core fact table for 2024/25.
resource: ../data/matches.csv
tags: [football, fact-table]
updated: 2026-06-19
---

# matches

Core fact table. 1,752 rows across the top-5 leagues.

## Schema
| Column | Type | Coverage | Notes |
|--------|------|----------|-------|
| `match_id`  | string | 100%  | Deterministic ID |
| `home_xg`   | float  | 99.9% | Expected goals (Understat) |
| `referee`   | string | 22%   | Only EPL has referee data |

## Joins
- `match_id` → [match_stats](match_stats.md) (1:2, perfect)
- `match_id` → [lineups](lineups.md) (1:~31, perfect)
Two things to notice. The frontmatter is filterable: an agent can ask “show me every type: Table updated this month” without reading the bodies. And the foreign key is written as a link — match_id → [lineups](lineups.md) — so the agent follows join paths the way you follow hyperlinks.


The frontmatter fields








Field
Required?
Use




type
Yes
Dataset, Table, Metric, Concept, …


title
No
Human label


description
No
One sentence the agent reads first


resource
No
Path or URL to the thing described (the CSV, the dashboard)


tags
No
Flat list for grouping


generated
No
Who wrote it and when, e.g. { by: "human:yourname", at: "2026-06-19T00:00:00Z" }


verified
No
Who checked it against the data, and when (same { by, at } form)

title: Knowledge Bases for Agents
section: A README vs. an OKF Bundle
text:
A README vs. an OKF Bundle
These are complements, not competitors. A useful way to see the difference:









README / single doc
OKF bundle




Audience
Human reading start to finish
Agent fetching one slice


Shape
One file, narrative
Many files, one per concept


Relationships
Described in prose
Encoded as markdown links


Best for
Project overview, setup, the “why”
Rich relational datasets with many tables



The honest guidance: don’t convert everything. A one-off script or a single CSV needs a good README, not a bundle. The payoff of OKF appears when you have a genuinely relational dataset — several tables with foreign keys — that an agent will query repeatedly over time. For that case, splitting a long data description into linked per-table files means the agent loads only what it needs and can walk the joins.

title: Knowledge Bases for Agents
text:
Maintaining It with AI
This is where it becomes practical rather than aspirational. Keeping cross- references current is exactly the chore that kills hand-maintained documentation — and exactly what an agent is good at. A workable loop:

Generate the first draft — point Claude Code at your data folder and ask it to draft one concept file per table, with schema and inferred join paths.
Verify against the data — the non-negotiable step. Check that column types, coverage percentages, and especially the join keys are real, not plausible inventions. (See the verification discipline in Documentation Fundamentals.)
Let the agent maintain it — when the data changes, ask the agent to update the affected files and fix every cross-reference in one pass.

The first draft is cheap; the verification is where your judgment earns its keep. An agent will happily write coverage: 100% for a column that is half empty.

title: Knowledge Bases for Agents
text:
Try It
For worked examples, browse the sample bundles in the OKF repository. Open one and notice how each table file links to the ones it joins, and how the top-level index.md carries the whole join map.

title: Git for working with agents
text:
Suppose we ask an agent to fix the date variable in our cleaning script. It does that, and while it is there, it also renames two columns, changes a filter in another script and rewrites part of the README. Ten minutes later the regression table has 312 fewer observations. Which of these changes did it? With Git, we can see every changed line, and go back with one command. Without Git, we have to remember.
This page goes deeper than the short Step 4.4: Keep a history of every change in the friendly introduction. For installing Git and GitHub Desktop, see Version control with Git and GitHub. The commands here work the same for R and Python projects, in any terminal (see Terminal Basics).
Checked against official documentation on 22 November 2026.

title: Git for working with agents
section: Why does Git matter more with an agent?
text:
Why does Git matter more with an agent?
When we edit code ourselves, we change one thing at a time and we know what we changed. An agent changes many files in one go, quickly, and sometimes more than we asked for. Its summary at the end describes what it meant to do, not necessarily what it did. The diff is the record of what it actually did: every line removed and every line added, file by file.
Git also makes it cheap to say no. If a change is wrong, we throw it away and ask again, and nothing is lost. This makes it easier to let the agent try things.

title: Git for working with agents
section: What is the minimum we need to know?
text:
What is the minimum we need to know?
Five ideas and a handful of commands are enough for most projects.








Idea
What it is
Command




Repository (repo)
A project folder whose history Git keeps
git init (once)


Commit
A saved snapshot of all files, with a one-line note. git add -A first marks all changes for the snapshot (staging)
git add -A then git commit -m "note"


Diff
The changes between two versions, line by line
git diff


Log
The list of past commits, newest first
git log


Restore / revert
Go back: throw away uncommitted changes, or undo a commit
git restore, git revert



Two more commands we use all the time: git status lists the files that changed since the last commit, and git diff --stat shows how many lines changed in each file. Look at --stat first. A one-line fix that touched 400 lines in six files deserves a question.
Older tutorials use git checkout for both going back and switching branches. Git now has two separate commands for these, git restore and git switch, and we use those here.

title: Git for working with agents
section: What is the routine for one agent task?
text:
What is the routine for one agent task?
1. Commit before the agent starts. We want a clean starting point, so everything the agent does shows up as its change. If git status says there is nothing to commit, we are already clean.
git status
git add -A
git commit -m "Before agent: fix date variable"
2. Give the task. One task per round. Small tasks give small diffs, and small diffs get read.
3. Read the diff. Start with the list of files, then read the lines.
git status
git diff --stat
git diff
Ask three questions. Did it change only the files it should have? Is there anything we didn’t ask for? Do the outputs still look right after rerunning the code?
4. Keep it or undo it. If the change is good, commit it with a note on what changed. If not, throw it away (see What do I do when it goes wrong?) and ask again with a better prompt.

title: Git for working with agents
section: Can the agent do the Git steps for me?
text:
Can the agent do the Git steps for me?
Yes. An agent that runs terminal commands can run Git too, and agents write good commit notes. The friendly introduction has three prompts for reviewing, committing and reverting (Let the agent run Git). A few more we use:

Before you start, run git status. If there are uncommitted changes, stop and tell me.


Show me git diff --stat, then explain the change in code/clean.R line by line. Flag anything that changes the number of observations.


Which commits since Monday touched code/regressions.R? For each, one line on what it changed.

The agent can summarize the diff for us, and it helps. But the summary is written by the same agent that made the change. It is good practice to read the diff ourselves, at least for the files that produce numbers we will report.

title: Git for working with agents
section: Where can I see the diff without the terminal?
text:
Where can I see the diff without the terminal?
Three tools show the same diff in a window, with removed lines in red and added lines in green.

GitHub Desktop. The Changes tab lists every file changed since the last commit. Click a file to see its diff. The History tab shows past commits and what each changed. Type a note in Summary and click Commit to main (the button names the current branch).
VS Code. Open the Source Control view with Ctrl+Shift+G (⌃⇧G on Mac). Changed files are listed under Changes. Select one to open its diff. The Source Control Graph shows the history, and the Timeline view in the Explorer shows the history of one file.
The Claude desktop app. After Claude changes files, click the line counts (such as +12 -1) in the Changes card, or select Changes, to see the diff file by file. Hover over a line and click the + next to its number to leave a comment. Claude reads the comments, makes the changes, and shows them as a new diff.

title: Git for working with agents
section: When should I use a branch?
text:
When should I use a branch?
A branch is a parallel line of history. We use one when the agent tries something we may not keep: a new specification, a different way to clean the data, a large rewrite of a script. The main line stays as it was until we decide.
git switch -c try-new-spec     # create the branch and move to it
# ... the agent works, we commit as usual ...
git switch main                # back to the main line, untouched
git merge try-new-spec         # keep the experiment
If we don’t want the experiment, we switch back to main and leave the branch alone. In GitHub Desktop, click Current Branch, then New Branch. To bring an experiment into the main line, switch to main, click Current Branch, then Choose a branch to merge into main.
The Claude desktop app can go one step further. In a Git repository, turn on Worktree before starting a session, and the session works in a separate copy of the project folder (a worktree) on its own branch, so our main folder stays untouched. Commit what we want to keep before archiving the session: uncommitted changes in a worktree can be lost.

title: Git for working with agents
section: What should never go into Git?
text:
What should never go into Git?
Two things: confidential data and secrets. Git remembers everything, so a file that was committed once stays in the history even after we delete it. A file called .gitignore in the project folder lists what Git should skip. A starting point for an R or Python project:
# data: kept out of Git
data/
*.dta
*.sav

# secrets
.env
.Renviron

# environments and caches
.venv/
renv/library/
__pycache__/
.Rhistory
.RData
Python users usually keep API keys in .env, and R users in .Renviron, which R reads at startup. Both must be in .gitignore before the first commit. GitHub keeps official templates for many languages at github.com/github/gitignore.
Note that .gitignore doesn’t affect files Git already tracks. To stop tracking one, run git rm --cached data/survey.csv, then add the rule. If a key has already reached GitHub, removing the file is not enough. Revoke the key at the provider and create a new one (see How to get an API key).
Why keep data out, even in a private repository? Raw data doesn’t change, so it doesn’t need a history. Data agreements often forbid copies on third-party servers. And GitHub blocks files larger than 100 MiB. Back up data separately and to commit the code that produces the clean data instead (see Reproducible Research).

title: Git for working with agents
section: Why put the repository on GitHub?
text:
Why put the repository on GitHub?
Git works on our own computer. GitHub keeps a copy of the repository online, private unless we choose otherwise. This copy survives a lost laptop, and a coauthor can see the same history. We send our commits there with git push, or Push origin in GitHub Desktop, for example at the end of each day. Setup takes a few minutes and is described in Version control with Git and GitHub.

title: Git for working with agents
section: What do I do when it goes wrong?
text:
What do I do when it goes wrong?
It depends on whether the bad change was committed. Here are the cases, from the most common.
The agent’s last change is not committed yet. Throw away the changes to tracked files:
git restore .
If we already ran git add, use git restore --staged --worktree . instead. Neither deletes new files the agent created, and git status still lists them. Delete them by hand, or ask the agent to. In GitHub Desktop, select the files in Changes and choose Discard Changes. Discarded changes go to the Trash, so they can still be recovered. In VS Code, right-click the file under Changes and choose Discard Changes.
We are still in the Claude Code session. Claude Code saves a checkpoint before each prompt. Type /rewind, or press Esc twice, pick the prompt, and choose Restore code. This is fast, but it doesn’t undo changes made by shell commands the agent ran, and it is no replacement for Git.
The bad change is already committed. Undo the last commit with a new commit that reverses it:
git revert --no-edit HEAD
HEAD means the last commit, and --no-edit keeps Git from opening a text editor. The history keeps both the mistake and the undo, so nothing is lost. In GitHub Desktop, right-click the commit in History and choose Revert Changes in Commit.
We want yesterday’s version back. Find the commit with git log (it shows the date of each commit) or in the History tab, and copy its short ID, such as a1b2c3d. To get back one file:
git restore --source a1b2c3d code/clean.R
To get back every tracked file as it was, use git restore --source a1b2c3d . and commit the result.






WarningAvoid commands that rewrite history



Agents sometimes suggest git reset --hard or git push --force. These change or delete history, and work can be lost for good. Before any Git command that undoes something, ask the agent what it will undo and wait. The two lines for AGENTS.md in the friendly introduction make this the default.

Key Definitions
Before diving in, let’s clarify terms that are often used interchangeably but mean different things:

title: Documentation Fundamentals
text:
About Markdown
Markdown is a lightweight markup language that’s become the standard for documentation in data science. It’s readable as plain text but renders nicely in browsers and editors.

Quick Markdown reference

**bold** and *italic*

title: Documentation Fundamentals
text:
What is a Good README?
A README is the front door to your project. Someone should be able to understand what your project does, how to use it, and where to find things—all from reading the README.

Key Ingredients
A complete README for a research project should include:

Overview — What is this project? What question does it answer?
Data sources — Where does the data come from? Any access restrictions?
File structure — What’s in each folder? Which scripts run in what order?
Requirements — Software, packages, and versions needed
Instructions — How to run the analysis from start to finish
License — Terms for reuse (MIT, CC-BY, etc.)
Contact — Who to ask questions



Data Description Checklist
For each dataset in your project, document:

Name and file format (csv, parquet, xlsx)
Number of observations and variables
Unit of observation (person, firm-year, country-month)
Time coverage and geographic scope
Key variables with brief descriptions
Missing data: how much and why
Data lineage: source → processing → final structure



Examples of Good READMEs
Reproduction packages

Békés-Kézdi (2021) Hotels dataset — clean, minimal, effective
Koren-Pető (2021) Business disruptions from social distancing | PDF version — comprehensive research package

Templates and guides

Make a README — interactive guide with examples
Social Science Data Editors Template — journal-standard template
AEA Data Editor guidance — requirements for top economics journals

title: Documentation Fundamentals
text:
What is a Codebook (Variable Dictionary)?
A codebook provides detailed, variable-level documentation. While the README gives the big picture, the codebook tells you exactly what Q47_recoded means.

What to Include for Each Variable



Element
Example




Variable name
income_hh


Label
Household monthly income


Type
Numeric (continuous)


Unit/metric
EUR, monthly


Valid range
0–999999


Coding for categories
1=Low, 2=Medium, 3=High


Missing values
-99 = refused, NA = not asked


Share missing
4.2%


Notes
Top-coded at 99th percentile





Examples of Good Codebooks

Békés-Kézdi (2021) Bisnode dataset variables — clean spreadsheet format
Reif (2022) Illinois Wellness codebook — plain text, version controlled
On earnings data – used in this course

title: Documentation Fundamentals
text:
Tips for AI-Assisted Documentation
LLMs can significantly speed up documentation, but require careful verification.
What AI does well

Summarizing long codebooks
Generating first drafts of variable descriptions
Suggesting what’s missing from your documentation
Converting between formats (e.g., codebook PDF → markdown table)

What requires human oversight

Verifying variable definitions match actual data
Checking that coded values (1, 2, 3…) match the stated meaning
Ensuring coverage statistics are accurate
Confirming data lineage is correct

A practical workflow

Start by having a first look to get a feel. Look at documensts, check the index. Open data.
Upload your codebook/data to the LLM
Ask for a structured summary
Verify 3-5 variables manually against the source
Iterate: ask AI to fix errors you find
Final human review before publishing

title: Decision logs, reviewing agent work, and disclosing AI use
text:
Ask an agent to clean a survey and run a wage regression, and twenty minutes later it has made a dozen choices for you. It dropped duplicate IDs, kept the respondents with a missing wage out of the sample, used log wages, trimmed the top 1 percent, and picked a type of standard error. Each choice may be fine. But you didn’t make them, and most of them are not visible in the results. This page is about three habits that keep such work under control: a log of decisions, a review before you trust the outputs, and a record of what the AI did, for yourself and for the journal.
Policies checked on 22 November 2026.

title: Decision logs, reviewing agent work, and disclosing AI use
text:
Part 1: The decision log

Why keep a decision log?
An agent doesn’t stop to ask about every choice. If it did, we couldn’t work with it. So it decides, quietly, and moves on: which rows to keep, how to merge two tables, what to do with missing values, which estimator options to use, what goes into the main chart. Reading the code finds some of these choices, slowly. A decision log puts all of them in one file.
The file is called DECISIONS.md and sits in the project folder. Every analytical choice gets an entry: what the decision point was, what alternatives there were, how it was decided, and why. It is good practice to log a choice when a reasonable analyst could have chosen differently and the choice could change the results or how we read them. Mechanical steps with no real alternative don’t need an entry.
If you followed the friendly introduction, you already have the decision-log skill, which keeps this file in the format of the examples below.


What goes into an entry?
The most useful field is the basis: who or what decided. Four answers cover most cases.







Basis
Meaning




user
You decided. Give the date.


evidence
The data decided: a check was run, and the entry names the numbers or the file.


convention
Common practice in the field. Name the source.


default
The agent chose, for convenience, and nothing was tested. Look at these first.



Each entry also has a status: needs-review (you haven’t looked at it yet), provisional (fine to make progress, to revisit later), or decided. Entries are numbered D1, D2, … and never deleted. A reversed decision gets a new entry, and the old one is marked superseded by Dn.
Here are two entries as they might look in a project on a school survey. The numbers are made up for illustration.
## D3 - Duplicate respondent IDs
- **Decision point:** 214 student IDs appear twice in the 6,480-row survey file.
- **Chosen:** For the 201 pairs with identical answers, keep one row (re-submitted
  forms). The 13 pairs with different answers are kept aside in
  data/clean/dup_conflicts.csv and left out of the sample for now.
- **Alternatives:** keep the first interview of each pair; keep the last; drop all
  428 rows (loses 214 students, 3% of the sample, for no reason in most pairs).
- **Basis:** evidence (output/checks.md: 201 of 214 pairs identical on all items).
- **Affects:** all tables; 13 students. Easy to reverse.
- **Status:** needs-review. The 13 conflicting pairs need a look at the field notes.

## D7 - Standard errors clustered by school
- **Decision point:** The tutoring program was assigned to whole schools (48 schools),
  so test scores of students in the same school are likely correlated.
- **Chosen:** Standard errors clustered at the school level in all regressions.
- **Alternatives:** HC1 standard errors (allow for heteroskedasticity but not for
  correlation within schools, so likely too small); clustering by class (treatment
  does not vary within school); wild cluster bootstrap (worth adding as a check,
  since 48 clusters is not many).
- **Basis:** user (YYYY-MM-DD), following the convention of clustering at the level
  where treatment is assigned.
- **Affects:** standard errors and confidence intervals in Tables 2-4; not the estimates.
- **Status:** decided.
Note what the first entry does. The agent found a problem, solved the easy part with evidence, and left the hard part to us, marked needs-review. This is the behavior we want.


How do I make the agent keep it?
Add one line to AGENTS.md, the file of standing instructions the agent reads at the start of every session:
- Any choice I did not specify goes into DECISIONS.md, marked needs-review.
The starter AGENTS.md of the friendly introduction already points to the decision-log skill. For more lines worth adding, see Step 4.2 of the friendly introduction
Then review the log at natural break points, say after cleaning and after the first estimates. Ask: “List the needs-review and default decisions in DECISIONS.md, starting with those that most results depend on.” Go through them one by one, and change the status to decided when you agree.

title: Decision logs, reviewing agent work, and disclosing AI use
section: Part 2: Reviewing agent work before trusting outputs
text:
Part 2: Reviewing agent work before trusting outputs

Why read the log before the results?
Once you have seen a nice coefficient, you judge every choice by whether it keeps the coefficient nice. That’s human. So read DECISIONS.md first, while you don’t know yet which choice helps. You did exactly this in Step 2.6 of the friendly introduction.


What checks should be in the code?
Checks that live only in a chat are gone tomorrow. Checks in the code run every time. It is good practice to have the agent write them into the scripts, and to save the results to a file after each run:
- Put checks in the code (row counts, duplicate IDs, merge matches, value ranges, missing values). After each run, save all checks with pass/fail in output/checks.md. If a check fails, stop and tell me.
A check is one line in either language. In Python, assert df["student_id"].is_unique. In R, stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(df$student_id)). The file then reads like this:
| Check                               | Expected | Found | Result |
|-------------------------------------|----------|-------|--------|
| Rows after import                   | 6,480    | 6,480 | pass   |
| Duplicate student IDs after D3      | 0        | 0     | pass   |
| Students matched to school register | >= 98%   | 96.1% | FAIL   |
| Test score range                    | 0-100    | 0-100 | pass   |
| Share missing in parental income    | < 10%    | 23.4% | FAIL   |
The two failures are not bugs to make go away. Each needs a decision, and so a log entry. For the different kinds of tests in a larger project, see Three kinds of tests.


Which numbers should I recompute myself?
Pick two or three numbers a reader will remember: the sample size, the mean of the outcome, the main estimate. Recompute them without the agent’s code, from the clean data, in a few lines of your own or in a spreadsheet. If your number matches, you have checked the whole chain behind it. If it doesn’t, you have found something worth an hour.


Should another agent review the work?
Yes, for anything that matters. The session that did the work remembers its own reasoning and tends to defend it. A fresh session doesn’t. Use the review prompt in Step 4.6 of the friendly introduction, which reruns everything from scratch. To focus on the choices, add: “For each decision in DECISIONS.md with basis default, say whether a reasonable alternative could change the main result.” A reviewer running on another provider’s model, for example Codex reviewing work done in Claude Code, is less likely to share the same blind spots.


What are the red flags?

The number of rows changes between steps, and no log entry explains it.
A check was edited, or a threshold loosened, in the same session in which it failed.
A whole-table dropna() or na.omit(), or missing values filled with zero.
Error handling that hides errors: a try with nothing in the except, or an R tryCatch() that returns NULL.
A number in the text or a table that no script produces.
A result much larger or much cleaner than in the literature.
“Done, all tests pass”, with no checks.md to show it.

title: Decision logs, reviewing agent work, and disclosing AI use
section: Part 3: Recording and disclosing AI use
text:
Part 3: Recording and disclosing AI use

What should I record about the model?
Write down which tool, which model, which version, when, and with which settings. Models are retired fast. Claude Opus 4, released in May 2025, was retired from the Claude API on 15 June 2026. Claude Sonnet 4.5, released in September 2025, is retired on 30 November 2026. OpenAI publishes a similar list. Once a model is retired, nobody can rerun your prompts on it, and the same prompt on its successor may give a different answer.
In Claude Code, /model shows the model in use, /effort status shows the effort level, and claude --version gives the version of the app. In other tools, the model menu shows the model. The setup page suggests noting the model and date in DECISIONS.md. For a longer project, a short table in docs/ai-use.md works better:
| Date       | Task            | Tool (version)      | Model           | Settings       | Transcript                   |
|------------|-----------------|---------------------|-----------------|----------------|------------------------------|
| 2026-11-22 | Cleaning, D1-D9 | Claude Code (x.y.z) | claude-opus-5-5 | effort: medium | logs/2026-11-22-cleaning.txt |


Should I keep the prompts?
Keep the ones behind results you will report. In Claude Code, /export logs/2026-11-22-cleaning.txt saves the current conversation as a text file. Elsevier, for example, asks authors to keep a record of which tool and model was used and how. A transcript may contain your data, so store it where the data may be stored.
When the model is part of the method, the prompt is part of the code. If a script sends 5,000 open-ended answers to a model to classify them, the prompt, the model name and the settings belong in code/, and later in the paper’s appendix. See LLM APIs in Python.


What do journals and funders require?
Policies differ in detail, but they agree on three points. An AI tool can’t be an author. The authors are responsible for everything AI produced. And AI use has to be disclosed, although where and how much differs.



Who
What they ask




AEA (AER editorial policy)
If AI was used to prepare the manuscript, including drafting or editing text, describe it briefly during the submission process. Authors are solely accountable for AI outputs and must fact-check them.


Science journals
Note AI use in the cover letter and in the methods or acknowledgments. Code that changes functionality, data generation or analysis: methods section, with model name and version. Drafting or translating text: acknowledgments, with model name and version. Language editing and literature searches: no declaration. AI-generated images only with the editors’ permission.


Elsevier
A section titled Declaration of generative AI and AI-assisted technologies in the manuscript preparation process, just before the references. AI used in the research, including for code: Methods section, with the name of the model, version and developer. Basic grammar and spelling checks need no declaration.


Springer Nature
An AI declaration in the manuscript: the AI system, the purpose, and how much it contributed. For analytical uses (data analysis, statistical modeling, qualitative coding), also the validation steps.


ERC (funder)
Applicants may get input from AI, but this doesn’t relieve them of full and sole authorship responsibility. The ERC’s position statement doesn’t ask for a disclosure.



The pattern, then: AI in the analysis or the code goes in the methods section, AI help with writing goes in a declaration or the acknowledgments, and polishing the language is sometimes exempt. Journals of the same publisher can differ, so read the author guidelines of your journal before you submit. For a thesis, check your university’s rules and ask your supervisor.


How do I write an AI-use statement?
Say which tool and model, when, for what, how you checked it, and who is responsible. A statement like this is easy to shorten for a submission form:
AI use statement. We used Claude Code (Anthropic) with the model Claude Opus 5.5
(claude-opus-5-5) between 3 and 21 November 2026 to write and debug the Python code
for data cleaning and estimation, and to edit the language of Sections 1 and 5.
All analytical choices made with the tool are listed in DECISIONS.md in the
replication package. We checked the code with automated tests, recomputed the main
estimates in Table 2 independently, and reviewed and edited all text. We take full
responsibility for the content of this paper.
Then move each part where your journal wants it: the analysis part to the methods section, the writing part to the declaration or the acknowledgments. The log and the checks file belong in the replication package, next to the README. See Documentation fundamentals.

title: Choosing a model with evidence
text:
Checked on 22 November 2026. Prices and model names change every few months, so check the sources at the end before you rely on a number.
Say we have 40,000 open-ended answers to the survey question “Why did you leave your last job?”, and we want each coded into one of five categories. At today’s list prices, this costs about $320 with Claude Opus 5.5 and about $8 with OpenAI’s gpt-6-luna (the calculation is below). Is the cheap model good enough? No leaderboard can tell us, because no leaderboard has seen our categories. This page shows how to find out with a small test of our own.
Which AI model shall we choose? gives an opinion on the leading models. Calling LLM APIs from Python advises using “the smallest model that passes your benchmark on real data”. This page is the how-to for that benchmark.

title: Choosing a model with evidence
text:
What do public leaderboards measure?
There are many leaderboards. Four are worth knowing, and each answers a different question.



Site
What it measures
How




Artificial Analysis
General ability, plus price, speed and cost per task
Runs nine evaluations itself, under the same conditions for every model, and combines them into an Intelligence Index


Arena (formerly LMArena)
Which answer people prefer
Users vote between the answers of two anonymous models, and the votes are turned into a score


SWE-bench
Fixing real software bugs
The model gets a code base and an issue from GitHub, and has to write a patch that fixes it


OpenRouter
Not a benchmark: prices
Lists the price of the same model at each company that runs it



Artificial Analysis also shows that “the model” is not one thing. Claude Opus 5.5 scores 35 at low effort and 58 at maximum effort, and the cost of one index task goes from $0.98 to $10.04. So when we compare models, we compare a model at a given effort setting.
Arena scores come from a Bradley-Terry model, a regression on who won each pairwise vote. Voters tend to like longer, nicely formatted answers, so Arena adds answer length and formatting to the regression (“style control”). Even so, a vote says which answer a person liked, not which answer was correct.

title: Choosing a model with evidence
text:
What do they miss?
They are a good way to draw up a shortlist. But there are three reasons why a high score may not carry over to our task.
First, contamination. If the test questions were in the training data, the score measures memory. In February 2026 OpenAI stopped reporting results on SWE-bench Verified, the 500-problem version of SWE-bench that many launch announcements used. All models it tested could reproduce the original human-written fix for some problems. It also found a second flaw: at least 59.4% of the problems it audited had tests that rejected correct solutions. This is also why Artificial Analysis now bases 60% of its index on private test sets or held-out answers.
Second, task mismatch. A coding or science benchmark says little about sorting survey answers into our codebook, or pulling the founding year out of company reports. Our categories have their own gray zones: is “my mother got ill and I had to care for her” a family reason or a health reason? Only our own rows test that.
Third, who ran the numbers. Launch announcements report benchmarks the vendor picked, run with the vendor’s settings. Independent runs, like those of Artificial Analysis, are better. They are still someone else’s task.
Prices need checking too. On OpenRouter, the input price of Kimi K3.1 Pro ranges from $0.24 to $4.40 per million tokens, depending on the company that runs it. For DeepSeek V4.1 Flash the range is $0.05 to $1.50. The cheapest provider may have other drawbacks, such as where your text is processed.

title: Choosing a model with evidence
section: How do we test a model on our own task?
text:
How do we test a model on our own task?
The idea is the same as checking a research assistant’s coding: we label a sample ourselves and count how often the model agrees. It takes an afternoon, and the steps below use the survey example.

Step 1: Label 100 rows by hand
Draw 100 answers at random and code them yourself, with the codebook you will give the model. Random matters: a sample of the easy cases flatters every model. If you can, ask a colleague to code 30 of them too. Where the two of you disagree, the codebook is unclear, and no model will do better than you on those rows.
Save the result as validation.csv with three columns: id, text, label. Keep these rows out of the prompt. If the model sees them as examples, the test is contaminated in the same way as SWE-bench.


Step 2: Pick three or four candidates
Choose one from each kind: a very good closed model, a mid-priced one, a cheap one, and an open-weights one. Give all of them the same prompt and the same effort setting. Through OpenRouter, one script can call all of them, with one key. Create the key on openrouter.ai, add a few dollars of credit, and save it as the environment variable OPENROUTER_API_KEY, as shown in Calling LLM APIs from Python.


Step 3: Run each model twice on the same rows
import os, datetime
import pandas as pd
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://openrouter.ai/api/v1",
                api_key=os.environ["OPENROUTER_API_KEY"])

MODELS = ["anthropic/claude-opus-5.5", "openai/gpt-6.2-sol",
          "deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash", "openai/gpt-6-luna"]
PROMPT = open("prompt_v1.txt").read()   # instruction + codebook
val = pd.read_csv("validation.csv")     # id, text, label

rows = []
for model in MODELS:
    for run in [1, 2]:
        for r in val.itertuples():
            resp = client.responses.create(model=model, input=[
                {"role": "system", "content": PROMPT},
                {"role": "user", "content": r.text}])
            rows.append({"id": r.id, "model": model, "run": run,
                         "pred": resp.output_text.strip().lower(),
                         "in_tok": resp.usage.input_tokens,
                         "out_tok": resp.usage.output_tokens,
                         "date": datetime.date.today().isoformat()})

res = pd.DataFrame(rows).merge(val, on="id")
res["correct"] = res["pred"] == res["label"].str.strip().str.lower()
print(res[res["run"] == 1].groupby("model")["correct"].mean())
Four models, two runs and 100 rows make 800 calls, which cost a few dollars at most. The response also reports how many tokens each call used. Save those too, and compute the cost from them rather than from a guess. In R, the ellmer package does the same job with chat_openrouter().


Step 4: Compare accuracy, stability and cost
Here is what the comparison could look like. The prices are real list prices on 22 November 2026. The accuracy figures are made up, to show how to read such a table.






WarningIllustrative: prices are real, accuracy is made up

Prices from Anthropic and OpenAI, and from DeepSeek’s own API at peak hours (off-peak is half). Cost per 1,000 rows assumes 1,000 input tokens per row (instruction, codebook and answer) and 200 output tokens (label, short quote, some thinking). “Weakest category” is the share of correctly coded answers in the category where the model does worst.


How do we read this? It is good practice to write down what “good enough” means before looking at the results. Say we decide on at least 90% overall and at least 80% in every category. Then three models pass, and the cheapest of them is DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. For 40,000 answers it costs about $22, against $320 with Claude Opus 5.5. gpt-6-luna is cheaper still, and its overall accuracy looks fine. But it gets only 7 of the 13 health answers right, so it fails.
Two cautions about the numbers. With 100 rows, one row is one percentage point. At 90% accuracy the standard error is about 3 points, so 95% against 94% is no evidence of a difference. Compare models on the same rows, and look at the rows where one is right and the other is wrong. Also, the cost column depends on tokens, and the same text is a different number of tokens for different models. Anthropic, for instance, says the tokenizer of its newer models produces about 30% more tokens for the same text than the earlier one. This is another reason to compute cost from the token counts your own run reports.


Step 5: Read the errors, not just the score
A cross-table of true and predicted labels, pd.crosstab(res["label"], res["pred"]) for each model, shows where the errors go. This matters more than the overall score. Errors spread evenly across categories add noise. Errors that pile up in one category bias the shares we report: in the table above, gpt-6-luna could understate the share of people who left for health reasons by almost half. Then read the wrong rows themselves. Some will be the model’s fault, and some will show that the codebook needs a sharper rule. If you sharpen the codebook, test the new version on 50 fresh rows: the rows you tuned it on now flatter it.


Step 6: Check stability
A model doesn’t always give the same answer to the same question. The column “Same label on re-run” compares run 1 with run 2:
wide = res.pivot_table(index=["model", "id"], columns="run",
                       values="pred", aggfunc="first")
print((wide[1] == wide[2]).groupby("model").mean())
The rows where the two runs disagree are usually the ambiguous ones, and they are the ones to read yourself. A model that changes 7 labels out of 100 between runs makes our results hard to reproduce, whatever its accuracy.

title: Choosing a model with evidence
section: What about agent and coding work?
text:
What about agent and coding work?
Agent work is harder to score row by row, but a smaller version of the same test works. Give two models the same small task, each in its own copy of the project folder. For example: “Read firms.csv and sales.csv, merge them on firm ID, and report how many rows did not match.” Decide the checks before you start. Does the script run? Is the number of unmatched rows the one you computed yourself? Did the agent ask before changing files? How long did it take? An application that works with many models, such as OpenCode, makes the switch easy. Part 5 of the friendly introduction has the setup and more tasks to compare.
One run of an agent task is a small sample. If the two models differ only a little, run the task again before drawing a conclusion.

title: Choosing a model with evidence
text:
Record what you used
Models are retired, and model names don’t always point to the same model. From 1 December 2026, Google will route all API requests for gemini-2.5-pro to Gemini 3.8 Flash. DeepSeek’s API name deepseek-flash is currently served by DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017, and will move on to a newer version at some point. OpenRouter has aliases such as ~openai/gpt-sol-latest, which follow the newest model.
So save, next to the results:

the exact model ID (deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash, not “DeepSeek”) and the provider,
the date of the run,
the effort setting and the prompt version,
the validation result: accuracy, weakest category, agreement between runs.

Keep validation.csv and the script. When a model is retired, or a cheaper one appears, rerunning the test takes minutes. For a frozen model that never changes, see Open-weights and local models and Running AI on your own computer.
