title: Part 2: First Steps
text:
2.1 Set the ground rules
Before class
Each session starts from zero: the agent doesn’t remember yesterday. So it is good practice to write down once what it should always know: who you are, how you work, and what it must never do. This file is called AGENTS.md. It sits in the project folder, and the agent reads it at the start of every session.
The second tool is a skill: a recipe for one type of task, written as a Markdown file called SKILL.md in its own folder. The agent uses a skill when the task matches its description, or when you type / and its name. We start with two.

read-pdf makes the agent extract a PDF’s text to a .txt file first and work from that, with page numbers. This prevents the most common failure with PDFs: answering from a partly read document without saying so.
decision-log records every analytical choice in a file called DECISIONS.md: dropped observations, variable definitions, methods. For each choice it notes the alternatives and the basis: evidence, convention, your instruction, or just a default.

We prepared both, and a starter AGENTS.md. One prompt sets everything up:

Download these three files exactly (use a download command, do not retype them):
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/gabors-data-analysis/da-w-ai/main/friendly-agentic-ai-intro/starter/AGENTS.md
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/gabors-data-analysis/da-w-ai/main/friendly-agentic-ai-intro/starter/skills/read-pdf/SKILL.md
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/gabors-data-analysis/da-w-ai/main/friendly-agentic-ai-intro/starter/skills/decision-log/SKILL.md

Save the first as AGENTS.md in this folder, and the two skills as .claude/skills/read-pdf/SKILL.md and .claude/skills/decision-log/SKILL.md.
Then create the folders that AGENTS.md describes, and summarize its instructions for me in five bullet points.

Then open AGENTS.md in Typora and edit the “About me” section. It is your file. Folders starting with a dot, like .claude, are hidden by default, so you may not see that one in Explorer or Finder.

It worked if you start a new session (+ or New session), type /, and both skills show up in the list.







NoteWhat is in the starter files (click to open)





AGENTS.md
# Instructions for the AI agent in this project

The agent reads this file at the start of every session. Edit it freely.
When the agent makes the same mistake twice, add a line here.

## About me

- I am a social scientist (EDIT: field, e.g. sociology, political science, economics).
- I have used AI as a chatbot, mostly for text. I have not written code before.
- Explain what you do in plain language. The first time you use a technical term,
  give a one-line definition.
- Use Python for code, unless I ask for R or Stata.

## How to work with me

- For any task with more than a few steps, first show me a short plan and wait for my OK.
- Do the smallest thing that answers my request. Ask before adding extras.
- Work in small steps. Stop at natural break points and tell me what you did and what is left.
- If my request is unclear, ask one question rather than guessing.
- When you finish, say what you did not do or could not check.
- Keep `status.md` up to date: what is done, what is open, what comes next.
  Update it at the end of each task. When I say "continue", read it first.

## Safety with my files

- Work only inside this project folder. If a step needs anything outside it, stop,
  tell me what and why, and wait for my OK.
- Never delete files. If something should go, move it to `_old/` and tell me.
- Never change anything in `data/raw/`. Raw data stays as it arrived.
- Never overwrite a Word, Excel or PDF file I gave you. Save your changes as a new
  file with `_v2` (or the next number) at the end of the name.
- Install Python packages only inside this project's environment (`.venv`).
  Ask before installing anything for the whole computer.
- Do not upload my files or data to any website or online service.

## Data and numbers

- Never make up numbers, references, quotes or sources. If you cannot verify something, say so.
- When you report a number, say where it comes from (which file, which script, which web page).
- Check your own results: count rows before and after each step, and compare a few
  values by hand with the source.
- Log analytical choices in `DECISIONS.md` (see the `decision-log` skill).
- Do every step that reads, changes or creates data in a script in `code/`, never as a
  one-off command. Start each script with a short comment in plain language: what it
  reads, what it does, and what it writes.

## Sources and quotes

- Work from the files in this folder, not from memory. If the answer is not in the
  files, say "not in the files".
- Every quote must be word for word from a file in this folder, with the file name and page.
- Every reference must be a file in this folder or have a DOI that opens.

## Folders and files

- `data/raw/` original data, never edited
- `data/clean/` cleaned data, produced by code
- `code/` scripts, numbered in the order they run: `01_get_data.py`, `02_clean.py`, ...
- `output/` figures (PNG) and tables
- `docs/readings/` papers as PDFs, with their extracted text; never edit the PDFs
- `docs/extracts/` one Markdown summary per paper
- `docs/` notes, memos and drafts. Write new text in Markdown (`.md`);
  convert to Word only when I ask.
- Every result must be reproducible: running the scripts in order rebuilds all outputs.

## Writing

- Plain, direct prose. Short sentences. No hype words (delve, crucial, landscape,
  comprehensive, shed light on).
- Say what the data shows, then the caveats. Talk about associations, not effects,
  unless the design allows a causal reading.

## PDFs

- To read a PDF, first extract its text to a `.txt` file, then work from the text
  (see the `read-pdf` skill).
The read-pdf skill
---
name: read-pdf
description: Read a PDF (paper, report, book chapter, questionnaire, codebook) reliably by first extracting its text into a .txt file and then working from that text. Use whenever the user asks to read, summarize, quote, compare or extract information or tables from a PDF.
---

# Read a PDF: text first

Reading a PDF directly is unreliable: long files get cut, columns get mixed up, and the
agent may answer from a partial view without saying so. So we always extract the text
first, save it, and work from the saved text.

## Steps

1. **Extract the text.** Use the Python package `pymupdf` in this project's environment
   (install it with the project's package manager if missing). Save the text next to the
   PDF with the same name and a `.txt` ending, for example `paper.pdf` -> `paper.txt`.
   Mark each page with a line like `=== page 7 ===` so page numbers can be cited.
2. **Check the extraction.** Report the number of pages and the number of characters.
   If a page has almost no text (under ~200 characters), it is probably a scanned image.
   For those pages, render them to PNG (150 dpi is enough) and read the images.
   Tell the user which pages were read as images.
3. **Work from the `.txt` file**, not the PDF. For long documents (more than ~40 pages),
   read it section by section rather than all at once.
4. **Cite page numbers** for every claim, number or quote taken from the document.
   Quote exactly; never paraphrase inside quotation marks.
5. **Tables:** when the user needs a table, copy it into a CSV in `data/raw/` and then
   check three numbers from the CSV against the page image.

## What to tell the user at the end

- what was extracted (pages, characters, any pages read as images)
- where the `.txt` file is
- anything that could not be read well (garbled tables, formulas, footnotes)
The decision-log skill
---
name: decision-log
description: Keep a DECISIONS.md log of the analytical choices made during data work (which observations to keep, how a variable is defined, which method, which chart), so the researcher can review the reasoning before trusting results. Use whenever cleaning data, building a sample, defining variables, choosing a method or designing a table or figure, even if the user does not mention it. Also use when the user asks "what did you decide?" or "review the decisions".
---

# Decision log

Every result rests on judgment calls the reader never sees. The researcher needs to
check those calls *before* looking at results. This skill keeps them in one file,
`DECISIONS.md` in the project folder, written as the decisions are made.

## What to log

Log a decision when a reasonable analyst could have chosen differently AND the choice
could change the results or how we read them. Examples:

- dropping observations (missing values, outliers, small groups, a year or a country)
- defining a variable (what counts as "employed", income in levels or logs, which year's prices)
- merging tables (which key, what to do with rows that do not match)
- choosing a method (mean or median, which regression, which controls)
- designing an exhibit (what goes in the main chart, what is left out)

Do not log mechanical steps with no real alternative, or formatting.

## Format

Create `DECISIONS.md` on first use. Keep a summary table on top and a short entry for each
decision below it. Number entries D1, D2, ... and never renumber or delete them.

```markdown
# Decision log

| ID | Date | Decision | Basis | Status |
|----|------|----------|-------|--------|
| D1 | 2026-11-06 | Drop respondents younger than 18 | user | decided |

## D1 - Drop respondents younger than 18
- **Decision point:** The survey includes 16-17 year olds; the question is about adult voters.
- **Chosen:** Keep age 18 and above (drops 412 of 9,870 rows).
- **Alternatives:** keep all (rejected: they cannot vote); keep 16+ (only where voting age is 16).
- **Basis:** user instruction, 2026-11-06.
- **Affects:** all tables and figures. Easy to reverse.
```

The **Basis** field matters most. Be honest about it:

- `evidence` a check was run (name the file or the numbers)
- `convention` common practice in the field (name the source)
- `user` the researcher asked for it (give the date)
- `default` chosen for convenience, not tested. This label is the most useful one for the
  reviewer, because it shows where to look first.

**Status** is `decided`, `provisional` (to make progress, revisit later) or `needs-review`.

## How to work

1. Write the entry when the decision is made, not at the end.
2. If a decision drops a lot of data, changes the main finding, or is hard to undo,
   mark it `needs-review` and tell the user in plain words before going on.
3. If a decision is reversed, add a new entry and mark the old one `superseded by Dn`.
4. When the user asks to review the log, list first the `default` and `provisional`
   decisions that many results depend on.



In short, AGENTS.md says: plan before longer tasks, do the smallest thing that answers the request, never delete (move files to _old/), never change raw data or your own files, work from the files and not from memory, quote word for word with the page, and keep a short progress note in status.md. Grow the file slowly. When the agent makes the same mistake twice, add one line.

Staying in charge: set the limits
The folder is a boundary. In Manual mode the agent asks before it reads or changes any file outside the project folder, and before it runs any command. Commands are the one gap: an approved command can reach anything you can. So read the paths before you click yes. Do you see a folder outside your project, such as C:\Users\you\Desktop or ~/Documents/other-project? Click no and ask: “Why do you need to go outside the project folder?”
AGENTS.md adds a rule on top: work only inside this folder, and ask before going outside it.
Which permission mode? Stay in Manual for the first week: you see every step. After that, we suggest a simple rule: free inside the project folder, permission everywhere else. In the app this is the Accept edits mode. The agent creates and edits files in the project folder without asking, but it still asks before running other commands and before touching anything outside the folder. If a project needs a second folder, add it with + next to the prompt box, then Add folder, and the same rule covers it. Leave Bypass permissions alone: it switches off the questions altogether.

title: Part 2: First Steps
text:
2.2 Collect the papers
In class · playtime
Every project starts with collecting material. Here the agent does the downloading and, more important, keeps a record of where each file came from. Start a new session and send:

Download the reading list from https://raw.githubusercontent.com/gabors-data-analysis/da-w-ai/main/friendly-agentic-ai-intro/starter/reading-list.md and save it as docs/reading-list.md.
Then download each paper on the list into docs/readings/, with the file name given. Try the PDF link first; if it fails, use the backup copy if there is one.
Check every file: is it really a PDF, and does its first page show the right title?
Write docs/readings/SOURCES.md: a table with the file name, the citation, the DOI, where you downloaded it from, today's date, and the licence.
Tell me which downloads failed and why. Do not try other websites.
Finally, make the PDFs read-only.

If you have time. The next prompt is slower, and it can wait until after class. Let the agent search on its own, with a tighter rule:

Find three more published papers on whether big events (sports, blackouts, disasters, holidays) change the number of births nine months later.
For each, give the full citation and a DOI, and open the DOI to check that it leads to that paper. Download a paper only if it is free to read.
Add them to docs/readings/SOURCES.md, marked "found by the agent". If you cannot confirm a paper, leave it out and say so.


It worked if the six papers open as papers in your PDF reader, and SOURCES.md lists them. If you ran the search, check the three new papers yourself: open each DOI in your browser and see that it leads to that paper.

Why the check that each file is really a PDF? When we prepared this pack, two of the downloads “succeeded” but saved a web page instead of a paper: one asked to enable JavaScript, the other said Oh no!. Both files were called .pdf. An agent that doesn’t check would happily summarize them.

Staying in charge: see what it did
You don’t have to take the agent’s word for what it did. After it creates or changes files, a Changes card shows the number of added and removed lines. Click it for the diff view: each changed file, with removed lines in red and added lines in green. It works like tracked changes in Word, for any file. You can also ask at any point: “List every file you created or changed in this session.”
To see every file read and every command run, switch the Transcript view to Verbose (press Ctrl+O to cycle through the views, or use the menu next to the session title).

title: Part 2: First Steps
section: 2.3 Make an extract of each paper
text:
2.3 Make an extract of each paper
In class · playtime
A good extract is a summary you can check. This time we agree on the checks before the work. Start a new session, switch the permission mode to Plan, and send:

Use the read-pdf skill on every PDF in docs/readings/.
For each paper, write docs/extracts/<file name>.md with: citation; research question; data (where, when, how many); method in one or two plain sentences; main finding; one sentence quoted word for word that states the main finding; the limitations the authors name. Give the page number for each item. If the paper does not state something, write "not stated". Do not use what you know about the paper from elsewhere.
Then write docs/extracts/overview.md: one table, one row per paper.
Before you start, tell me how you will check your own extracts.

Read the plan. A good answer includes at least this: every quote is searched for, word for word, in the extracted text, and every page number is checked. If the plan doesn’t say so, ask for it. Then switch back to Manual and let it go ahead.
Then check it yourself. Open docs/extracts/overview.md in Typora.

Pick two papers. Open each PDF at the page given and search for the quoted sentence (Ctrl+F, or Cmd+F on a Mac). Is it there, word for word?
Pick one paper and read its abstract. Does the extract say the same?
Look at one “not stated”. Is it really not in the paper?

Why the fuss about quotes? Summarizing is what these models do best, and the table will look convincing. The typical mistake is a different one: a paraphrase presented as a quote, or a finding that comes from the model’s general knowledge and not from the file. A page number and a word-for-word quote make both mistakes easy to catch. In a published paper, a quote that doesn’t exist is the kind of error readers remember.

Staying in charge: agree the checks before the work
For work with text, three checks cover most mistakes: every quote is found word for word at the page given, every reference is a file in the folder or has a DOI that opens, and every number matches the table it comes from. For data, the checks are counts of observations, duplicates, value ranges and missing values (Step 2.6).
Then let the agent report by exception: it runs the agreed checks and tells you only about failures. But “no problems found” means only that the agreed checks passed. Keep your own hand check of two quotes. It takes five minutes, and it is the one check that doesn’t depend on the agent.

title: Part 2: First Steps
text:
2.4 Ask the papers questions
In class · playtime
Now the folder is a small library, and you can ask it questions. Start a new session and try these, one at a time.

Using only docs/extracts/ and the papers in docs/readings/: which papers find more births after a big event, which find fewer, and which find no change? Group them, and give author, year and page for each claim.


Do the answers depend on how long the event lasts, an evening or several weeks? Use only the papers in this folder, with pages.

Then a test. Ask a question that the papers cannot answer:

What do these papers say about births in Argentina after the 2022 World Cup?

None of the papers covers it. The right answer is “not in the files”. If the agent answers anyway, from memory, you have just seen why the rule in AGENTS.md matters. Tell it, and ask where each claim came from.
Finally, ask for documentation. A folder of papers is only useful later if you know what is in it.

Write docs/readings/README.md: what this folder contains, how the extracts were made, a one-line description of each paper, and what the collection does not cover.


Staying in charge: the folder, not the memory
The model behind the agent is not a database. It doesn’t look facts up, it reconstructs them, so a reference or a number it “remembers” can be wrong. It is much stronger with material you put in front of it. So when you ask questions, say where the answer should come from (“using only the papers in docs/readings/”), and ask for the page. An answer you can trace to a page you can check. An answer from memory you can only believe.

title: Part 2: First Steps
text:
Debrief
Ten minutes, together. Three questions.

Did all six downloads work? Did anyone’s agent save a web page as a PDF, and did it notice?
Did your two quotes check out? Was any “quote” a paraphrase, or on another page?
What did the agent say about Argentina? Did it say “not in the files”, or did it answer from memory?

title: Part 2: First Steps
text:
After class: Steps 2.5 and 2.6
About an hour, at your own pace. Step 2.5 finishes the project of this part. Step 2.6 is a separate assignment, on a new question, for those who work with data. Both are also the first step of Part 4, the guide to the weeks after.

title: Part 2: First Steps
section: 2.5 Write the memo, review it, revise it
text:
2.5 Write the memo, review it, revise it
After class
This is the loop of every paper: a draft, comments, a revision. The agent writes the draft. You comment on it, on paper, as you would on a colleague’s draft. The agent sorts your comments, makes the language changes, and asks you about the rest.

Draft
Start a new session and send:

Write a one-page memo in docs/memo.md for a colleague in another field: "Do big events change when babies are born? What the research says."
Use only docs/extracts/ and the papers in docs/readings/. Cite as (Author year, p. X).
End with one paragraph on what this evidence cannot tell us.
Then convert it to docs/memo.docx.

If you have a Word file whose look you like, such as your university template, put it in docs/ and add: “Use docs/my-template.docx for the styles.” The agent copies its styles, not its text.


Review on paper

Open docs/memo.docx in Word and save it as a PDF: File → Save As, then choose PDF as the file type. Call it memo.pdf.
Open memo.pdf in your PDF reader: Microsoft Edge on Windows, Preview on a Mac, or Adobe Acrobat Reader anywhere.
Read it as you would a colleague’s draft. Highlight text and add comments. Make at least three comments on language (a clumsy sentence, a word you would change) and at least two on content (a claim you doubt, a missing caveat, a paper that is misread).
Save it as docs/memo_reviewed.pdf.



Revise

Read all comments, highlights and other annotations in docs/memo_reviewed.pdf (use pymupdf). List each one: the page, the marked text, and my comment.
Sort them into two groups: language and content.
Make the language changes in a copy of the memo, docs/memo_v2.md. Do not change the content yet.
Then ask me about each content comment, one at a time, and wait for my answer before you change anything.
When we are done, make docs/memo_v2.docx.

Then let Word show what changed. In desktop Word, go to the Review tab, click Compare, then Compare… (Windows) or Compare Documents (Mac). Choose memo.docx as the original and memo_v2.docx as the revised document. Word shows each change as a tracked change.

It worked if the agent’s list has every comment you made, the language changes changed only language, and the content changes are the ones you agreed to.







TipThe same loop on your own work



It works on any PDF with comments: a draft your coauthor marked up, a supervisor’s notes on a chapter, the proofs from a journal. It also works on a Word file with a coauthor’s tracked changes and comments: “List the tracked changes and comments in docs/draft_coauthor.docx, sorted into language and content.” But keep confidential material out of the folder until you have checked your data agreement (Step 1.2).








NoteWhy Markdown first, Word at the end? (click to open)





Right-click a Word file and open it with Notepad (on Windows). What you see is unreadable: a .docx is a packed bundle of files. Before the agent can work with it, it has to unpack and convert it, which costs time and loses some structure. A Markdown file reads the same in Notepad as in Typora. So we advise drafting and revising in Markdown with the agent, and converting to Word at the end. The idea comes from Simon Martin’s slides Jump-starting AI agents.




Staying in charge: keep the final say
The agent did the mechanical part: finding your comments, sorting them, fixing the language. The content decisions stayed with you, one at a time. It is your name on the memo, not the agent’s.
For anything that matters, add a second pair of eyes. The session that wrote a text is not its best judge: it remembers its own reasoning and tends to defend it. A new session has no such history. Start one and send: “You are reviewing docs/memo_v2.md, written by someone else. Check every citation against docs/extracts/ and the page given. List anything wrong or unsupported, most serious first. Do not change any files.”

title: Part 2: First Steps
text:
2.6 A first task with data
After class · a separate assignment
This is a separate assignment. It leaves the papers behind: a new question, and numbers this time. The question is simple: in EU countries where more women work, do women also hold more seats in parliament? If you don’t work with data, you may skip this step. Part 3 shows data work at a much larger scale.
Start a new session and, before you send the prompt, switch the permission mode to Plan.

Using the World Bank's open data (its API, no key needed), get for all EU countries for 2023:
- the share of seats held by women in the national parliament (%)
- the female labor force participation rate (% of women aged 15 and over)

Save the raw download in data/raw, write the code in code/, and make one scatter plot (participation on the x axis, seats in parliament on the y axis, with country labels) saved in output/.
Then write a half-page memo in docs/memo_data.md: what the chart shows, and three caveats.
Keep the decision log as you go.

Read the plan, and say plainly if something looks off. When you are happy with it, switch back to Manual and tell the agent to go ahead.
Then check it. This is your job, not the agent’s.

Open the chart. Are the countries where you expected them to be?
Pick two countries and look up their numbers on data.worldbank.org. Do they match the CSV file in data/raw?
Read DECISIONS.md. The World Bank has more than one measure of labor force participation. Which one did the agent pick, and did it tell you? Which countries had no 2023 data, and what did it do about them?
Read the memo. Does it say “effect” or “causes”? It shouldn’t. A scatter plot of 27 countries shows an association.

If you find a mistake, tell the agent, and add a line to AGENTS.md if it could happen again.

Staying in charge: the choices it made without asking
Note what happened in check 3. The agent made a choice that you didn’t know existed. Nothing is wrong with that, as long as the choice is written down and you read it. This is what the decision log is for: read DECISIONS.md before you trust the results.
You don’t need to read Python to follow the code. Click a script in the chat to open it, and ask: “Explain code/02_clean.py paragraph by paragraph, in plain language, for a colleague who doesn’t code.” Then ask about anything that sounds like a choice: “Why drop those rows? What else could you have done?”

title: Part 2: First Steps
text:
What did you practise?
Four ways of staying in charge, each tied to a step.









What it means
Where




Limits
The agent works in one folder, asks before it acts, and never changes your originals
Steps 2.1, 2.2


Visibility
You can see every file it changed, every step it took and every choice it made
Steps 2.2, 2.6


Checks
You agree the checks before the work, you say where answers must come from, and you check a few things by hand
Steps 2.3, 2.4, 2.6


The final say
The agent does the mechanical part; you decide the content
Step 2.5









NoteSix habits




Plan first. For anything longer than a few minutes, use Plan mode. It is much cheaper to fix a plan than to fix finished work.
Small steps. Ask for one thing, check it, then ask for the next. An agent running on a vague task produces plausible-looking work that you then have to read.
Work from the folder. Put the material in the folder and ask the agent to use it, with pages. Don’t rely on what the model remembers.
Check against the source. Compare a few numbers and a few quotes with the source by hand, every time.
One session per task. Long sessions get muddled. What must carry over goes in a file: standing rules in AGENTS.md, analytical choices in DECISIONS.md, and where the work stands in status.md. End a session with “Update status.md.” Start the next with “Read status.md and continue where we left off.”
Ask it to explain. “Why did you do that?” “What could go wrong here?” You are responsible for the work, so you need to understand it.

title: Part 2: First Steps
text:
Troubleshooting







Problem
What to do




The skills don’t show up when I type /
Start a new session. Skills load when a session starts


A downloaded “PDF” won’t open, or shows a web page
The site sent a web page instead of the paper. Ask the agent to use the backup copy, or download that paper yourself in the browser


A PDF comes out as nonsense, or nearly empty
It is probably a scan. Tell the agent, and the read-pdf skill reads those pages as images. Check such papers with extra care


The agent finds none of my PDF comments
Make sure you saved the PDF after commenting. Some readers keep comments in a separate file until you save


Word Compare shows changes everywhere
The agent probably rebuilt the whole document. Ask it to start again from a fresh copy and change only the text


The agent seems stuck, or keeps doing the wrong thing
Click stop and say plainly what you want. If the session is long, start a new one


It made a mess of my files
Ask: “List every file you created or changed in this session.” Then ask it to move the unwanted ones to _old/


An error I don’t understand
Paste it in and ask: “Explain this error simply, then fix it.”



More setup problems: Part 1. Unfamiliar terms: the glossary in the overview.

title: Part 2: First Steps
text:
What comes next?
So far we went step by step, one task at a time. In Part 3 we do the opposite: we give the agent a single prompt and watch it write a whole paper. Its question is close to yours from this part: does the World Cup change the number of births? The agent was told to ignore the literature. You have just read it, which makes you a well-prepared referee.

title: Friendly Introduction to Agentic AI for Social Scientists
text:
A mini course in six parts


Friendly Introduction to Agentic AI for Social Scientists


From a chatbot that polishes your text to an AI agent that works with your files: your readings, your Word drafts, your data
Version 0.9 · 27 November 2026

title: Friendly Introduction to Agentic AI for Social Scientists
text:
Who is this course for?
You are a social scientist: a sociologist, a political scientist, an anthropologist, an economist. You have used ChatGPT or Claude in a browser, mostly to improve a text or as a better search engine. You haven’t used it for the actual work of your field, and you may never have written a line of code. This course is for you. Seniority doesn’t matter.
When I say you should experiment with agentic AI, I hear two typical reactions.
“This is for coders.” It isn’t. You won’t type a single command. You give instructions in plain language, as you would to a research assistant. Even the technical setup is done by the agent, which explains each step before it takes it.
“I don’t need this.” Maybe. The course lets you find out on your own material. You remain in charge, and you decide how much to delegate. You will see what an agent can do and how to supervise it. At the very least, you get a glimpse.
We use one tool: Claude Code, in the Claude desktop app, on Windows, Mac or Linux. Codex by OpenAI is the most similar, and what you learn here carries over fully. Antigravity, with Google’s Gemini, is also similar, and there are close alternatives that run open-weights models. But when learning, one tool is enough.

title: Friendly Introduction to Agentic AI for Social Scientists
text:
What is an AI agent?
Let’s start with what you know. A chatbot is a conversation in a browser. You paste in a text or upload a file, it answers, and you copy the answer back into your document. It knows only what you gave it in that conversation. It mostly relies on information it “remembers” from its training, which can be wrong. It cannot read your files, run code, or save results.
An agent is the same AI model with four additions. First, it has access to folders on your computer: the ones you allow. Second, it can act there: open files, write and run program code, save results. Third, it works in a loop: it takes a step, looks at the result and decides on the next one, until the task is done or it needs you. Fourth, it can use tools: open a browser, or call other programs such as Microsoft Word.


  
    
      
    
    
      
    
  
  

    
    Chatbot
    what you know

    
    You

    
    Chatbot
    in a browser

    
    Your files

    paste a text in
    
    
    copy the answer out

    out of reach

    

    
    Agent
    what this course adds

    
    You

    
    Agent
    on your computer

    
    One folder
    that you choose

    a task, your OK
    
    
    questions, results

    reads, runs, saves
    
    
    looks at the result
    again and again, until done
  

The model is the same. The difference is where it works and what it is allowed to do.

The loop makes the difference. Suppose you ask for a chart of turnout by age group from survey.csv. A chatbot needs the file uploaded and may guess what the columns mean. The agent does the following:

it opens the file and sees that age is called age_cat, not age;
it writes a short program and runs it;
it hits an error because some ages are coded “refused”, and asks you how to handle them (or makes an assumption you can check);
it runs the program again, opens the chart to check it, and saves it in output/.

You see every step, and at first it asks your permission before each one.
It helps to think of the agent as a very fast research assistant sitting at your computer. It has read a lot, but it is new to your project, and it can be wrong with confidence. Hence your job shifts from doing each step to instructing the agent and checking its work. Checking matters most.
One more point changes how you use it. The model behind the agent is not a database. It doesn’t look facts up in its memory, it reconstructs them, so a reference, a number or a date it “remembers” can be wrong. It is much stronger at working with material you put in front of it. So working with an agent is largely about designing its context: you provide the grounding material (your readings, your data, your notes) and the tools to search and compute, and you ask it to work from those rather than from memory. A table of readings built from the PDFs in your folder can be checked line by line. One built from what the model recalls cannot.
Indeed, the right habit is to make it write code that can be run directly, and notes that can be searched directly.

title: Friendly Introduction to Agentic AI for Social Scientists
section: What can it do for a social scientist?
text:
What can it do for a social scientist?
Here are a few tasks that fit an agent well. None of them needs you to write code.


Hundreds of historical notes, as OCR-ed PDFs. Many large PDFs in a folder first become plain text, which can then be searched and turned into a data table.


A draft in Word. The agent comments on the argument, or edits a copy, and you review each edit as a tracked change.


Paper review. A detailed review of a draft, with agents that check the numbers, the references and the argument. The agent reads the literature, places your work in it, and suggests journals.


Data analysis. The agent downloads data, cleans it, runs regressions, makes tables and charts, and writes a first-pass report that describes the data. You check the code and the results.


Prototype. You have an idea. The agent does the first pass: literature, data, code and a draft. Then you decide whether it is worth your time to continue.


The agent has limits, too. First, the agent makes mistakes, and it makes them in fluent, confident prose. It may misread a variable, drop observations without telling you, or hand you a paraphrase in quotation marks. Second, it doesn’t know the judgment calls of your field: which cases belong in the sample, or what a concept means in your literature. Third, what it reads is sent to the company’s servers, so confidential material needs care.
Each of these problems has a routine that handles it, and you already know most of them from supervising research assistants and refereeing papers. Part 2 builds them into every step.

title: Friendly Introduction to Agentic AI for Social Scientists
text:
Worried you will break something?
Many people are, and it is a good instinct. Here is why you can relax.

Nothing happens without your click. In Manual mode, where we start, the agent asks before it changes a file or runs anything. When in doubt, click no. Nothing bad follows from a no.
It works in one folder you choose. Your other files are outside it. If a request ever names another folder, click no and ask why.
Start with copies. Put copies of your files in the project folder and keep the originals where they are. In the worst case, you delete the folder and start again.
You can stop it at any time. The stop button interrupts it mid-step.
You can ask before you approve. “What does this do? Is it safe? Can it be undone?” The agent answers in plain language.
You can’t run up a bill. Pro has a fixed monthly price. When you reach the usage limit, the agent pauses until the limit resets, unless you choose to buy extra usage.
Even the Python setup can be undone. The agent writes down what it installed and how to remove all of it (Step 1.4).

title: Friendly Introduction to Agentic AI for Social Scientists
text:
What do you need?

A paid Claude plan. Claude Code needs Claude Pro or higher (about $20 a month, cancel any time; see pricing). A university Claude Team or Enterprise plan also works. ChatGPT Plus includes OpenAI’s Codex, the closest alternative. Antigravity, with Google’s Gemini, is similar. See Which plan do I need?
A computer with Windows 10 or 11, macOS, or Linux (Ubuntu or Debian).
Permission to install software. A university laptop may need IT approval. Try first, and ask if you are blocked.

title: Friendly Introduction to Agentic AI for Social Scientists
text:
How is the course organized?
The course has six parts and an assignment. The first two parts are hands-on: setup takes about an hour, the first project about two. The third is a live demonstration. The assignment follows it: you read the agent’s paper as a referee would, and you improve its prompt with skills. The fourth part is a guide to the weeks after: you make the rules and the skills yours, and you run a project on a question of your own. The fifth is broader advice for later, on other uses and other models. The sixth is a short list of links on where social science research may be heading. If something fails along the way, nothing is broken: check the troubleshooting table of that part, or ask the agent what went wrong.






TipTaking this as a two-hour workshop?



Before the session (at home, about an hour): Part 1, and Step 2.1.
In the session (two hours): at the start we give the agent the World Cup prompt of Part 3, and it works in the background. The first hour is Part 2: we explain a few ideas, you work on Steps 2.2 to 2.4 on your own laptop, and we end with a short debrief. The second hour is Part 3: the prompt, what it leaves out, and what the agent produced.
After the session (homework): Steps 2.5 and 2.6 of Part 2, and the Assignment on the World Cup project folder we share. Part 4 is for the weeks after, and Parts 5 and 6 for later.




1



Steps 1.1–1.5 · about an hour

Setup
Install the app, make a project folder, meet the agent, let it set up Python, and install a reader for the files it writes.
You end with a working agent in a folder of your own.




2



Steps 2.1–2.6 · an hour in class, an hour after

First Steps
One small project on one question: do big events change when babies are born? The agent collects six papers, makes an extract of each, answers your questions, and writes a memo. You review the memo on paper, and it revises. Then a short task with data. Each step ends with how to stay in charge: limits, visibility, checks, and the final say.
You end with extracts you verified on the page, a reviewed memo, and work you can put your name on.




3



Live demo

A Paper in 50 Minutes
We give the agent a single prompt, “Does the World Cup affect fertility?”, and watch it produce a short empirical paper and a slide deck. While it works, we look at the prompt: what it asks for, and what it leaves out.
You end with a view of a whole project, from one prompt to a paper.




A



Tasks A.1–A.2 · after the session

Assignment
Two tasks on the World Cup project. Read what the agent left behind as a referee would: the paper, the decisions memo, the code, the references. Then download six more skills and rewrite the prompt with them, so that the next run checks itself.
You end with referee notes on the agent’s paper, and a better prompt.




4



Steps 4.1–4.6 · the weeks after

After the Course
You are home. What next? A guided path that stays with the World Cup project: finish what is open, turn what you found as a referee into rules and skills of your own, then run your improved prompt on your own question and review the result.
You end with rules and skills that fit your work, and a first draft on a question from your own field.




5



Broader advice · for self-study

Go Further
No steps here, only advice for the time when the agent is part of your work: other things to use it for, making it write like you, an app that works with any model, and which model fits which task.
You end with a sense of what else to try, and of which tasks need the strongest model.




6



Links · updated as they come

AI in Science
A few links that peek into the future of social science fields: economics, political science, survey research, psychology. Each comes with a two- or three-sentence summary.
You end with a sense of where research in your field may be heading.

title: Friendly Introduction to Agentic AI for Social Scientists
text:
A short glossary

Agent: an AI model that acts on your computer (reads files, runs code, saves results) in a loop until a task is done.
Prompt: the instruction you type for the agent. In this course, prompts to copy come in boxes.
Session: one conversation with the agent. Each session starts fresh.
Context window: what the model can see at once. Long sessions fill it up, and quality drops.
Permission mode: how much the agent may do without asking you. We start with Manual: it asks every time.
Markdown (.md): plain text with a few formatting symbols. It is the common language of people and agents.
AGENTS.md: your standing instructions, which the agent reads at the start of every session.
Skill: a recipe file the agent follows for one type of task.
Terminal: a text window for typing commands. The agent uses one behind the scenes. You don’t have to.
Environment (Python): a project’s own copy of Python and its add-ons, kept in the .venv folder.
Harness: a word you will hear later. It is the program around the model that gives it these abilities. Claude Code is one.

title: Friendly Introduction to Agentic AI for Social Scientists
text:
Useful links
Many people have written about agents for researchers. These are the ones we find most useful for this audience.
For people who don’t code

Chris Blattman, AI for Professionals Who Don’t Code. A political economist’s guide to running projects, meetings and everyday academic work with an agent.
Mushtaq Bilal, A Beginner’s Guide to Claude Code for (Non-Technical) Academics. Written for the humanities and social sciences. The link is a summary; the original is a long post on X.
Carl Vellotti, Claude Code for Researchers. Interview transcripts, PDFs and field notes, with good advice on verifying quotes.
Neal Caren, social-data-analysis. Ready-made skills for qualitative and quantitative sociological research, from interview analysis to literature synthesis.

If you work with data

Paul Goldsmith-Pinkham, Claude Code for Applied Economists. Eight video episodes, from getting started to verification.
Scott Cunningham, Claude Code Changed How I Work. A long series on empirical research with an agent. Some posts are for subscribers.
Anton Korinek, AI Agents for Economic Research (August 2025). The latest in his series in the Journal of Economic Literature on using AI in economic research.
Mihail Velikov, AI in Business & Economic Research. One-page summaries of more than 180 guides and papers.

Background reading

Ethan Mollick, One Useful Thing. The best running commentary on working with AI.
Our own list: suggested readings and resources.

Official documentation

Claude Code: desktop app · skills · AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md · data usage

On this site, when you want more

Week 1: LLMs, Harnesses & Setup explains what is behind the chat box, and covers other agents.
Week 2: From Raw Data to Report is a full analysis project with an agent.
Glossary of LLM terms · Which AI model · AI Coding Prep

Setup


Install the Claude desktop app, make a project folder, meet the agent, and let it set up Python for you

title: Part 1: Setup
section: What do we do in this part?
text:
What do we do in this part?
Before a new research assistant can help, they need a desk, access to the right files, and the tools of the job. The agent is no different. In this part we install the app, make a folder for the agent to work in, have a first conversation with it, and let it install its own tools.
New here? Read the overview first: it explains what an agent is and what you need.


The five steps in one minute. No sound. Open it full screen

This part takes about an hour. The agent explains each step before it takes it, and you approve. If something fails, nothing is broken. See the troubleshooting table at the end, or ask the agent what went wrong. Worried you will break something? The overview explains why you can relax.






NoteWhat you will have at the end




The Claude desktop app, with the Code tab working
A project folder that the agent can read and write
Python, set up by the agent for you
A Markdown reader for the files the agent writes

title: Part 1: Setup
text:
1.1 Install the Claude desktop app






NoteWhich plan do I need?



The free Claude plan has no agent. For this course you need Claude Pro: $20 a month, or $17 a month paid for a year. You can cancel any time, so one month is enough to try. Prices as of November 2026; see claude.com/pricing.

Usage limits. Every plan has a limit that resets every five hours, and a weekly one. Long sessions, large files and the strongest models use it up faster. When you hit it, you wait until it resets. Pro is enough for this course and for light regular use.
More usage. Max ($100 a month) gives five times the usage of Pro, and Ultra ($200) more still. Move up only when you keep hitting the limit.
Through your university. Ask whether it has a Claude Team or Enterprise plan. These include the agent, and conversations on them are not used to train models. On Pro and Max, training is a setting you choose in your account’s privacy settings.
The alternatives cost about the same: ChatGPT Plus ($20) includes OpenAI’s Codex, and Google AI Pro (about $20) raises the limits of Antigravity, which also has a free tier. See the box below.




WindowsMacLinux



Download the installer: Claude for Windows. (On a Surface or other ARM laptop, use the ARM64 installer.)
Run the downloaded file. If Windows shows a blue “Windows protected your PC” box, click More info → Run anyway.
Open Claude from the Start menu and sign in with your Claude account.




Download the installer: Claude for macOS. It works on Intel and Apple Silicon Macs.
Open the downloaded .dmg file and drag Claude into Applications.
Open Claude from Applications (or press Cmd+Space, type Claude) and sign in.



The desktop app for Linux is in beta, for Ubuntu and Debian. Follow the steps on the official page: Claude Desktop on Linux. Then start Claude from your application launcher and sign in.
On another distribution, use the terminal version of Claude Code: install guide. The rest of this course still applies. You type the same prompts in the terminal.



Then open the Code tab at the top of the left sidebar (hover over the icons if you see no names). If it asks you to upgrade, your plan doesn’t include Claude Code.






TipChat or Code?



The Chat tab is the chatbot you know. The Code tab is the agent. Don’t let the name mislead you: Code is for any work on files in a folder, text included.








NoteUsing Codex or Antigravity instead? (click to open)





Two agents work much like Claude Code. Most of this course carries over: the project folder, AGENTS.md, planning first, small steps, and checking.
Codex, by OpenAI. The closest alternative. It comes with every ChatGPT plan: Free and Go include limited use, Plus and higher give more.

Install the ChatGPT desktop app, which now includes Codex. OpenAI’s instructions have the download links. On Windows it comes from the Microsoft Store.
Sign in with your ChatGPT account and open Codex.
Open your project folder, and start with the setting that asks before every action.
Codex reads AGENTS.md by itself, so our starter file works as it is. Skills live in a different folder: ask Codex where to put them.

Antigravity, by Google. It runs Google’s Gemini models. It is free to start, with weekly limits; Google AI Pro raises them. It looks more like a programmer’s editor than a chat window.

Download it from antigravity.google (Mac, Windows, Linux).
Sign in with your Google account.
Open your project folder, and choose the setting where the agent asks for your review before it acts.
Ask the agent to read AGENTS.md at the start of each session, or copy its rules into the tool’s own rules.

In both, the prompts of this course work as they are. The menus and the names of the settings differ, and they change often. When in doubt, ask the agent itself: “How do I make you ask before every action?”

title: Part 1: Setup
text:
1.2 Make a project folder
The agent works inside one folder. Think of it as the desk you give to a new research assistant: what is on the desk, they can read and work on. What is not, they can’t. Everything for a project lives there: data, code, notes, drafts, outputs. It is good practice to use a new folder for each project.

In your Documents folder, or in your Dropbox (see the box below), create a folder called ai-projects, and inside it a folder called first-project.
Use short names without spaces or accents (first-project, not My First Project (ÁÉ)). Programs handle plain names better.
Show file extensions, so you can tell .md, .csv, .py and .docx files apart.

Windows: in File Explorer, click View → Show → File name extensions.
Mac: in Finder, open Finder → Settings → Advanced and tick Show all filename extensions.








TipPut the folder in Dropbox



If you use Dropbox, OneDrive or Google Drive, it is good practice to create ai-projects there rather than in Documents. These services keep earlier versions of each file. So you can go back in time: if the agent spoils a file, open its version history and restore yesterday’s version. How far back you can go depends on your plan.
Git and GitHub do the same job more precisely, with a saved snapshot after each step that works. They take some setup. See Step 4.4 in Part 4.


Open the folder in Claude. In the Code tab, find the row of controls under the prompt box. Click the first one (the environment) and choose the top entry under Local. Then click the folder control next to it, choose Open folder… and pick first-project.






WarningWhat not to put in the folder (yet)



The agent sends what it reads to Anthropic’s servers. So keep confidential material out of the folder until you have checked your data agreement: interview recordings and transcripts, identifiable survey data, health records, anything under a data-use agreement, other people’s unpublished work.
In the EU, the GDPR applies: interview transcripts and survey answers about people who can be identified are personal data, even when names are replaced by codes, and sending them to an AI company needs a legal basis and safeguards. Only fully and irreversibly anonymised data falls outside it. Ask your university’s data protection officer before using such material, and see the European Commission’s What is personal data?.
Also check your Claude account’s privacy settings, which control whether your conversations may be used to train future models. For more, see AI and your data. For learning, public data and your own drafts are fine.

title: Part 1: Setup
section: 1.3 Have a first conversation with the agent
text:
1.3 Have a first conversation with the agent
Set the permission mode (in the row under the prompt box) to Manual. The agent then asks before it creates or changes any file and before it runs anything. True, this is slower. But you see everything, and that is what we want at the start. We advise staying in Manual for your first week. Next to the permission mode is the model picker. Leave the default for now: we come back to it in Which model should you use?
Type this and press Enter:

Hi. I am new to this. What can you see in this folder? Then create a file called hello.md with three sentences about what you can do for a social scientist.

The agent looks at the folder (it is empty), then asks to create a file. Read what it wants to do. If it is unclear, click no and ask: “What does this do? Explain in one sentence.”
Then try four things.

Click hello.md in the chat. It opens inside the app.
Ask: “Make it two sentences and less formal.” The agent edits the file, not just the chat.
The next time it asks to change the file, click no, on purpose. Nothing changes, and the agent waits for your instruction.
Click the stop button to interrupt it. You can also type a correction while it works.

Note the second one. With a chatbot, you would get a new version in the conversation and copy it over. Here the file itself changed.

title: Part 1: Setup
section: 1.4 Let the agent set up Python
text:
1.4 Let the agent set up Python
This is the most technical step of the course, and you don’t need to follow the details. It takes five to ten minutes. Read the one-sentence explanation before each command, then approve.
Why Python, if you work with text? The agent uses small Python programs as its tools: to read Word and PDF files, to convert formats, to handle large datasets and to draw charts. Python is free, it runs on every computer, and AI models write it well. You won’t write any of it yourself.
Copy this prompt into the agent:

I have never used Python. Please set up Python for this project folder.

- Use uv (a modern Python installer) to install Python and create an environment for this project only. Do not change anything else on my computer without asking.
- Before each command, tell me in one sentence what it does.
- Install these packages: pandas, matplotlib, openpyxl, pyreadstat, pymupdf, python-docx, pypandoc-binary, requests.
- Test it: write a short script code/00_test.py that makes a simple bar chart of five made-up numbers and saves it as output/test_chart.png. Run it.
- Finally write docs/SETUP-NOTES.md: what you installed, where it lives, how to run a script, and how to undo all of it.

What do the packages do? pandas handles data tables, matplotlib draws charts, openpyxl reads Excel, pyreadstat reads Stata and SPSS files, pymupdf reads PDFs, python-docx reads and edits Word files, pypandoc-binary converts between Markdown and Word, and requests downloads data from the web.

It worked if output/test_chart.png shows a bar chart. Keep docs/SETUP-NOTES.md: when something breaks months later, show it to the agent first.







TipIf something goes wrong here (click to open)






Windows: if the agent says it needs Git, install Git for Windows with the default options, restart the Claude app, and ask the agent to continue.
Mac: a window may ask to install command line developer tools. Click Install, wait a few minutes, then tell the agent to continue.
“Command not found” right after an install: quit the Claude app fully and open it again.
In every case, paste the error into the chat and ask: “What went wrong? Explain simply, then fix it.”




Already use Stata or R? Keep using them for your analysis: the agent can write and run do-files and R scripts, too. But do this step anyway, because the agent needs Python for its own tools.






TipAlready use R and RStudio? (click to open)





Keep them. You only need to decide which language does what.
Python stays, as the agent’s toolkit. The skills of Part 2 read PDF and Word files with Python, and so does the review loop of Step 2.5. So do Step 1.4 as written. Python lives in the project’s .venv folder and doesn’t touch your R setup.
R does the analysis. Change one line in AGENTS.md. Replace
- Use Python for code, unless I ask for R or Stata.
with
- Use R for data analysis, tables and charts. Use Python only for reading and converting PDF and Word files.
Make sure the agent finds R. The agent doesn’t work through RStudio. It runs R scripts with Rscript, the command-line version of R. On Windows, R is often not on the system path, and then the agent can’t find it. Ask once:

Find Rscript on this computer and tell me which version of R it is. Add its full path to AGENTS.md. Then write code/00_test.R that makes a bar chart of five made-up numbers, saves it as output/test_chart_r.png, and run it.

Keep RStudio as your editor. Open the agent’s .R scripts in RStudio, run them line by line and change them as you always do. If you change a script, tell the agent, so it knows your version is the one that counts.
Optional: renv. If you use renv, R’s way of keeping a separate set of packages for each project, ask the agent to set it up for this folder. It does for R what .venv does for Python.
The data task of Step 2.6 then comes out in R.

title: Part 1: Setup
text:
1.5 Install a Markdown reader: Typora
The agent writes its notes, memos and plans in Markdown: plain text files ending in .md, where a few symbols do the formatting (# Title for a heading, **word** for bold, - item for a list). Agents read and write it very well, and the files open on any computer.
To read Markdown as formatted text, install Typora. It looks and edits like Word, runs on Windows, Mac and Linux, and costs about $15 once, after a free trial.
A free alternative is Zettlr, made for academic writing. It is open source, runs on Windows, Mac and Linux, and exports to Word.

Download and install Typora from typora.io.
Open hello.md from Step 1.3 in Typora (right-click the file → Open with → Typora). It should look like a formatted document.
Make Typora the default program for .md files, so a double-click opens it.







NoteIf you write code, or plan to



Use VS Code instead (free). It previews Markdown and also shows the agent’s Python, R or Stata code. The main course uses it.

title: Part 1: Setup
text:
Which model should you use?
This section is for later. For Part 2 the default model is fine, so you may skip it now and come back when you plan a longer task.
The Claude app offers several models, and they differ in strength, speed and price. You choose in the model picker, toward the right end of the row under the prompt box. You can change the model in the middle of a session, too.
Our advice is simple. Start with the default, and change only when you have a reason.



Model
What it is
Use it for
Price




Opus (5.5)
The default. A strong model for work that needs reasoning
Almost everything in this course: extracts, the memo, the data task
1


Sonnet (5.5)
Faster and lighter
Routine work with a clear instruction: reformatting, tidying files, simple edits
about half


Haiku (5.5)
The smallest and fastest
One simple step repeated many times, such as sorting short texts into categories
a small fraction


Fable (5.2)
The strongest model, and the slowest
The hardest and longest tasks: a whole project from one prompt, as in Part 3, or the review of a finished paper
about twice



The price column compares Anthropic’s list prices per unit of text with Opus (November 2026). With a subscription you don’t pay per task, but the price shows up in another way: the stronger the model, the faster you reach your usage limit. Fable is special. On the Pro plan it is paid from usage credits, and on Max it is included up to half of your weekly limit. Model names and versions change every few months, so the picker may show newer ones.
When should you change?

Go up to Fable when the task is long and has many steps, or when the default got the same thing wrong twice.
Go down to Sonnet or Haiku when you keep hitting your usage limit, or when the task is simple and you repeat it many times.

Two more points matter for researchers.
A stronger model is not a substitute for checking. Every model can misquote a paper or drop observations without saying so. The checks of Part 2 apply to all of them.
Write down which model you used. Models are replaced and retired, and the same prompt gives a different result with another model. For anything you may publish, note the model and the date, for example in DECISIONS.md. You would do the same for the version of a statistical package.






NoteOther settings worth knowing




Effort. In the model picker, under Effort, you set how hard the model thinks before it answers: low, medium, high, xhigh (extra high) or max. The default is medium. Lower is faster and uses less of your limit. We suggest medium for this course, and high for work where a mistake is costly, such as the data task or a review. Max is rarely worth it.
Thinking. The current models always think before they answer, and there is no switch for it. To read the thinking, set the Transcript view to Thinking.
The usage ring. Next to the model picker, a small ring shows how much of your plan’s usage you have used. Click it for the details.
Permission mode. Manual for now (Step 1.3). For what to choose later, see Step 2.1.
Long sessions. What the model can see at once is limited, and a long session fills it up. Start a new session for each task. Part 2 shows how to carry over what matters.



Want to use models from other companies, such as cheaper open-weights models? See Part 5. For a comparison of the main models, see Which AI model in the knowledge base.

title: Data Analysis with AI
text:
A course in eight sessions · Gábor Békés, CEU


Data Analysis with AI


Five weeks of core material and a three-session capstone, for students who know data analysis or econometrics and want to rework their practice around AI

title: Data Analysis with AI
text:
What’s this
A course for students who already know data analysis / econometrics and want to seriously rework their practice around AI. The aim is not “tips and tricks”: it is to spend a semester building real things with AI as a teammate, and to think honestly about where it helps, where it lies, and where it lets you do work you genuinely could not do alone.
As AI becomes more and more powerful, it is also important to provide a platform to discuss human agency in data analysis. A core role of the instructor is to lead that discussion across the term — what we delegate, what we keep, and how we stay accountable for the result.
This is the 2026 Summer edition release
Last updated: 2026-07-10

Structure
The course is eight 200-minute sessions — a five-week core course plus a three-session capstone:

Week 1 — LLMs & Setup. The one front-facing week: what LLMs are, context windows and document sharing, free vs paid subscriptions, the model-vs-harness distinction, closed vs open-weights models — and getting a working harness (desktop + CLI) running.
Weeks 2–3 — Core Data Analysis. Use AI on tasks students mostly can do unaided: a reproducible raw-data-to-report pipeline, then reviewing and debugging AI’s work with instruction files, skills, and tests.
Weeks 4–5 — Research with AI. AI as a research companion: causal identification (controls, instruments, difference-in-differences) and text-as-data with LLM APIs.
Capstone (3 sessions). A team project that pushes students into work they have never done before: production-style web scraping, text-as-data classification using LLM APIs, and modern causal econometrics (difference-in-differences with staggered treatment, event-study designs). The whole point is that AI makes this newly accessible — and the course makes students actually do it.

Each week opens with a 30–60 minute “Before you come to class” checklist and ends with a deliverable due Sunday 23:55.


AI and me
At the end of all classes, instructors and students should always consider these three questions.

How did AI support me do what I planned.
How did AI fail me: gave half-truths, buggy code, imprecise arguments
How did AI extend me: helped do things I could not, or gave new ideas

title: Data Analysis with AI
text:
Course description

Content — the core course
Weeks 1–5 cover using large language models (LLMs — ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Le Chat and others) to carry out tasks in data analysis: LLM and harness setup, a reproducible raw-data-to-report pipeline, reviewing and debugging AI’s work, using AI as a research companion for controls/IV/DiD, and text-as-data on football interviews.
Several case studies run across the material — simulated hotel data from Austria, the World Values Survey, US CPS earnings, football manager post-match interviews. There are practice assignments and a learning-more collection with blogs, papers, and video recommendations.


Content — capstone
A three-session team project on manager changes in football. Each team picks a country, builds a 10+ season match-and-manager panel, scrapes news around each change, uses an LLM API to score how expected each change was, then runs a difference-in-differences analysis with heterogeneity by manager type, team, and expectation.
The capstone deliberately requires three things students typically have not done:

Web scraping at project scale — RSS feeds, article pages, hundreds to thousands of items across sources and languages.
Text-as-data with LLM APIs — designing a classification prompt, structured outputs, hand-validation against the model, cost and reproducibility.
Modern causal econometrics — staggered DiD, event-study specifications, parallel-trends diagnostics, anticipation effects.

The argument of the course is that AI is what makes this scope realistic in three sessions — and the capstone is where students prove that to themselves.


Background: data analysis / econometrics
You need a background in Data Analysis / Econometrics, a good introductory course is enough. I, of course, suggest Chapters 1-12 and 19 of Data Analysis for Business, Economics and Policy (Cambridge UP, 2021). Full slideshows, data and code are open source. But consider buying the book!🤝
In particular, the course builds on Chapters 1-6 and 7-10, and 19 and 22-24 of Data Analysis but other Introductory Econometrics + basics of data science knowledge is ok.


Background: coding
Students are expected to have some basic coding knowledge in Python or R (Stata also fine for the early weeks). The capstone is realistically Python or R only — scraping and API work in Stata is painful.


Relevance
AI is everywhere and has become essential, most analytic work will be using it. It’s like the Internet a while back. Does not solve all problems, but almost all intellectual tasks will rely on inputs from it.


Learning Outcomes
By the end of the course, students will be able to

Use genAI fluently across the standard data-analysis stack — wrangling, description, reporting, light text analysis.
Work with agentic CLI tools (Claude Code and similar) on a real repo, with reproducibility and tests.
Scrape structured data from the web for a defined research goal.
Use an LLM API to turn text into numbers, including prompt design, structured output, and hand-validation.
Run a modern difference-in-differences / event-study analysis with staggered treatment and discuss its limits honestly.
Distinguish AI uses where the output is fine as-is from those that need strong human supervision.
Run a multi-week team project from data collection to causal analysis, using AI throughout.



Target audience
The course is aimed primarily at graduate and advanced-undergraduate students in economics, quantitative social science, political science, sociology, business analytics, and adjacent fields — students who have done a real econometrics or data-analysis course and now need to reset their practice around AI. The capstone in particular assumes you are willing to push past your current toolkit.
The material is also designed to be forkable by instructors: all open source under CC BY-NC-SA, so teachers can pick weeks, swap case studies, and run their own version. Practitioners, researchers, and journalists with the background can absolutely go through it solo.

✅ Pre-class checklist

text:
Learning objectives
By the end of this session your team will:

title: Capstone Project — Session 2: From Text to Expectations
section: Today’s task — purpose and expected output
text:
Today’s task — purpose and expected output


🎯 Purpose


Starting example. Read this article before going any further: Reuters — “Last season we lose that game”, says Man United’s Amorim (1 Nov 2025). Amorim talking after a 2–2 draw, a year into his tenure at Man United. Does the press suggest a change is coming? How would you score this one?
That is the task — at scale.
For every manager change in your panel, produce a numeric expectation score that answers one question:

In the period before the change was announced, how strongly did the press suggest that a change was coming?

You are not trying to judge whether the new manager is good, nor whether fans are happy. You are measuring how much of a surprise the change was at the moment it happened.




📤 Expected output


Two datasets
article-level list. One row per article:



column
what it is




news_uid
unique id for the article


team
team the article is about


date
article publication date


score
LLM-produced expectation score



team–gameweek panel. Aggregate to one row per (team, gameweek) with two key variables:







column
what it is




team
team the article is about


date
article publication date


avg_score
average expectation score across articles in the window


n_articles
how many articles fed that average.



This is the object you merge onto your match + manager-change panel in Session 3. We will use lagged values of this score.
information on what you did

prompt_classifier.md
EXTRA: validation note (hand-labelled n, agreement rate).







Note



What counts as a “gameweek”? Default to a calendar week, because that is how football coverage is paced. But the unit of time is a choice — it can be shorter (a few days, if you want to see the signal tighten as the change approaches) or longer (a fortnight or month, if article volume is thin). Pick one, document it, and keep it consistent across teams.

title: Capstone Project — Session 2: From Text to Expectations
text:
Intro talks (~75 min)
Two short decks frame the session — watch/skim before the session if you can.


🎞️ 1. NLP Basics — Text as Data (~30 min)


Slides: NLP Basics — Text as Data
Walks the classical pipeline (tokenization → BoW → TF-IDF) and the modern tools (word embeddings, BERT, LLMs) — all on a running example: a Ruben Amorim post-match quote that looks a lot like the articles you’ll score.
Source text for both decks: Reuters — “Last season we lose that game”, says Man United’s Amorim (1 Nov 2025).




🎞️ 2. Scoring News with LLMs


Slides: LLM Scoring
The project-2 deck. Uses the same Amorim quote to answer: “What is the probability the manager is out in 4 weeks?”
Covers:

What the LLM is actually doing when it outputs a number — and three biases to expect.
Six prompting strategies — crude, anchored, structured JSON, reason-then-score, self-consistency, logprob-based.
In-class activities: pick a strategy and argue for it; score the Amorim article by hand before asking Claude.
Bonus task (3 p): investigate calibration.
Open design issues for the group to decide (temperature, hand-validate, output format, model choice, aggregation, time window).

title: Capstone Project — Session 2: From Text to Expectations
section: APIs: what you need this session
text:
APIs: what you need this session
APIs come up twice in this session: news/data APIs (to get articles) and LLM APIs (to classify them). You already saw these in Week 5 — Text as Data; the key references are in the Knowledge Base.


🔑 Getting set up



Get an API key (OpenAI, Anthropic, or similar): How to get AI API keys.
Budget ~$5 — that is more than enough for a project this size.
Store the key outside the repo. Use an environment variable (.env, export) — never commit it.
Test first. Run your classification prompt on 10–20 articles before you unleash it on 1,000.





📚 Reference reading


Pulled into our knowledge base so you can find it after the course:

Introduction to APIs — what an API call is, headers, auth, rate limits.
Calling LLM APIs from Python — practical first calls, response schemas, and model choice.
How APIs work under the hood — idempotency, retries, batching, tokens.
Simple walkthrough: World Bank + FRED — public data APIs.
Football-data walkthrough (FBref) — scraping a sports data source.

If you are new to APIs, spend 15 minutes on “Introduction to APIs” before you start your work block. If you already understand the basics and need to build the classifier script, start with “Calling LLM APIs from Python”.

title: Capstone Project — Session 2: From Text to Expectations
text:
Work tasks (2-hour block)


🔍 News collection & classification pipeline


1. Find news sources

Aim for ≥ 2 credible outlets per country.
Think about English vs local language news outlets.
Prefer sources with RSS or a simple URL pattern — you’ll thank yourself tomorrow.
Mix national and league-specific / tabloid and broadsheet: drama lives in tabloids, context lives in broadsheets.

2. Build URL/article lists

Google News RSS (with a manager name in the query) is the fastest start.
If the source has team-specific RSS feeds, prefer those.
Expected scale per season: ~20 teams × 2 sources ≈ 200–1,000 articles / season.

3. Scrape clean text

Title + lead + full body. Keep source + pubDate + URL for reproducibility.
Store in a single tidy table: one row per article.

4. Classify via LLM API

Call an LLM (OpenAI, Anthropic, …) via API to score each article
Consult AI on how to create a prompt for such an exercise.
Design a clear prompt — think about:

What scale or label set best captures “expectation”?
How should irrelevant articles be handled?
What output format makes downstream parsing easiest?

Prefer a structured response schema over free text, so each call returns the same fields, for example score, reason, and is_relevant.

extra - Validate before scaling: hand-label ~20 articles yourself, run them through the prompt, and compare. Aim for ≥ 80 % agreement; if you’re below that, revise the prompt before classifying the full set.
5. Aggregate

create team*gameweek panel with average score and article count per (team, gameweek)




Scale & reality check


📐 Plan before you scrape





Dimension
Example




Seasons
10


Manager changes per season
~30


Articles per change
~5


Total articles to classify
~1,500


Cost at typical pricing
A couple of dollars



This is a lot of work for a 2-hour block. Scope down on purpose:

Start with 1 season, 1 source and a 3-month window.
Get the full pipeline working end to end.
Only then expand.

Discussion

Coverage — Which manager changes got lots of press? Which got none? What does silence mean here?
Classification quality — Where did the model disagree with you on hand-labelled cases? Why?
Prompt engineering — Share one prompt change that noticeably improved output.
Cost & reproducibility — How many articles did you classify? What did it cost? Could somebody else rerun it from your repo?
Into Session 3 — Is your (team, change_date) → expectation_score table ready to merge into the panel?
